metadata.title: The Polynomial Method Strikes Back: Tight Quantum Query Bounds via Dual Polynomials

extraction_notes.note: The proof of Theorem 37 (thm:upper) has no proof environment and runs through Sections 3-3.4.2; emitted as two prose proof parts (the WLOG reduction in Sec. 3 and the final construction of r(x) in Sec. 3.4.2). The constructions of Sec. 3.4.1 are kept as their own definitions and lemmas, not as a third proof part.

Theorems 1-6 are informal introduction versions of later formal theorems that differ in content (hidden N=O(R) requirement, n vs R). They are kept as separate main nodes, each with a uses edge from the formal result(s) that establish it, not merged via also_stated_at.
The \newtheorem{fact} environment (Fact 48) states a cited combinatorial identity, so it is typed theorem with origin external rather than claim (Hard rule 4).
The two approximate-degree variants are marked external standard (uncited); the paper calls only its notation non-standard, so paper origin would also be defensible.
Proposition 50 is given without proof; the paper says only that its proof is implicit in prior work, so it is marked origin external.

The three-step proof overviews at the start of Sections 4 and 5, the NOR warm-up discussion in Sec. 3.2, the tables and the reduction diagram, and the intro survey of prior bounds (apart from a few cited results the paper states in full) are not nodes.
The definition of F^prop and F^{<=N} is one node over three sentences and an align* display, because the two symbols are introduced together and defined by a single display.

nodes.statement: The approximate degree of a Boolean function $f \colon \{-1, 1\}^n \to \{-1, 1\}$, denoted $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f)$, is the least degree of a real polynomial $p$ such that $|p(x)-f(x)| \leq 1/3$ for all $x \in \{-1,1\}^n$.
nodes.name: Approximate degree

nodes.statement: In 1998, Beals et al.~\cite{beals} observed that the bounded-error quantum query complexity of a function $f$ is lower bounded by (one half times) the approximate degree of $f$.
nodes.name: Polynomial method lower bound (Beals et al.)
conclusions: the bounded-error quantum query complexity of a function $f$ is lower bounded by (one half times) the approximate degree of $f$

nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a power of two and $N \geq R$, and let $n=N \cdot \log_2 R$.
nodes.name: Input size n

nodes.statement: We let the \emph{frequency} $f_i$ of range item $i \in R$ denote the number of times $i$ appears in the input list.
nodes.name: Frequency of a range item

nodes.statement: Recently, Sherstov~\cite{sherstovpersonal} showed an upper bound of $\tilde{O}(n^{3/4})$ on the approximate degree of this function.
nodes.name: Sherstov's upper bound for Surjectivity
conclusions: showed an upper bound of $\tilde{O}(n^{3/4})$ on the approximate degree of this function

nodes.statement: The approximate degree of $\mathsf{ SURJ}$ is $\tilde{\Theta}(n^{3/4})$.
nodes.name: Approximate degree of Surjectivity (informal)
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity has approximate degree $\tilde{\Theta}(n^{3/4})$.
conclusions: The approximate degree of $\mathsf{ SURJ}$ is $\tilde{\Theta}(n^{3/4})$
nodes.label: thm:introsurj

nodes.statement: Later, Belovs introduced a beautiful new framework for designing quantum algorithms~\cite{belovsframework} and used it to improve the upper bound for $k$-distinctness to $O(n^{3/4-1/(2^{k + 2} - 4)})$ \cite{belovs}.
nodes.name: Belovs' k-distinctness algorithm
conclusions: improve the upper bound for $k$-distinctness to $O(n^{3/4-1/(2^{k + 2} - 4)})$

nodes.statement: For any $k\geq 2$, the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-distinctness is $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{3/4-1/(2k)})$.
nodes.name: k-distinctness lower bound (informal)
conclusions: the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-distinctness is $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{3/4-1/(2k)})$
nodes.label: thm:introkdist

nodes.statement: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of Image Size Testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
nodes.name: Image Size Testing lower bound (informal)
conclusions: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of Image Size Testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$
nodes.label: thm:imagesize

nodes.statement: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-junta testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{k})$.
nodes.name: k-junta testing lower bound (informal)
conclusions: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-junta testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{k})$
nodes.label: thm:juntatesting

nodes.statement: There is a constant $c > 0$ such that the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the statistical distribution of a distribution over a range of size $n$ from the uniform distribution over the same range to additive error $c$ is is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
nodes.name: Statistical distance from uniform lower bound (informal)
nodes.statement_short: Approximating statistical distance from uniform to constant additive error needs approximate degree / quantum queries $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
conclusions: There is a constant $c > 0$ such that the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the statistical distribution of a distribution over a range of size $n$ from the uniform distribution over the same range to additive error $c$ is is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$
nodes.label: thm:sdu

nodes.statement: There is a constant $c > 0$ such that the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the Shannon entropy of a distribution over a range of size $n$ to additive error $c$ is is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
nodes.name: Shannon entropy approximation lower bound (informal)
nodes.statement_short: Approximating Shannon entropy to constant additive error needs approximate degree / quantum queries $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
conclusions: There is a constant $c > 0$ such that the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the Shannon entropy of a distribution over a range of size $n$ to additive error $c$ is is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$
nodes.label: thm:introentropy

nodes.statement: For any constant $\delta \!>\! 0$, there is an AC$^0$ circuit with approximate degree $\Omega(n^{1-\delta})$.
nodes.name: Bun-Thaler AC^0 approximate degree lower bound
conclusions: there is an AC$^0$ circuit with approximate degree $\Omega(n^{1-\delta})$
nodes.section: 1.2 Prior Work on Lower Bounding Approximate Degree
nodes.label: thm:mainthm

nodes.statement: For any Boolean functions $f$ and $h$, $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(h \circ f) = O\left(\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(h) \cdot \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f)\right)$.
nodes.name: Sherstov's robust composition theorem
conclusions: $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(h \circ f) = O\left(\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(h) \cdot \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f)\right)$
nodes.section: 1.2 Prior Work on Lower Bounding Approximate Degree
nodes.label: thm:robust

nodes.statement: Every range item has frequency at most $T$, for a specific threshold $T=O(N^{1/3}) \ll N$.
nodes.name: Bounded-frequency condition
nodes.label: cond

nodes.statement: A dual polynomial that witnesses the fact that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(f_n) \geq d$ is a function $\psi \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \{-1,1\}$ satisfying three properties: \begin{itemize} \item $\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n}\psi(x) \cdot f(x) > \varepsilon$. If $\psi$ satisfies this condition, it is said to be \emph{well-correlated} with $f$. \item $\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} |\psi(x)| = 1$. If $\psi$ satisfies this condition, it is said to have $\ell_1$-norm equal to 1. \item For all polynomials $p \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ of degree less than $d$, we have $\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0$. If $\psi$ satisfies this condition, it is said to have \emph{pure high degree} at least $d$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Dual polynomial witness
nodes.statement_short: A dual witness for $\widetilde{\deg}_\varepsilon(f)\ge d$ is well-correlated with $f$, has unit $\ell_1$-norm and pure high degree at least $d$.

nodes.statement: As is standard, we say that a function $f(n)$ is in $\tilde{O}(h(n))$ if there exists a constant $k$ such that $f(n)$ is in $O(h(n) \cdot \log^k(h(n)))$.
nodes.name: Soft-O notation

nodes.statement: For $1 \le T \le n$, let $H^n_{\leq T}$ denote the subset of $\{-1,1\}^n$ consisting of all inputs Hamming weight at most $T$. We use $|x|$ to denote the Hamming weight of an input $x \in \{-1,1\}^n$, so $H^n_{\leq T} = \{x \in \{-1,1\}^n \colon |x| \leq T\}$.

nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \{-1,1\}^n$. The $\varepsilon$-\emph{approximate degree} of a Boolean function $f : \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\}$, denoted $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(f)$, is the least degree of a real polynomial $p : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $|p(x) - f(x)| \le \varepsilon$ for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $|p(x)| \le 1 + \varepsilon$ for all $x \in \{-1,1\}^n \setminus \mathcal{X}$. We use the term \emph{approximate degree} without qualification to refer to $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f) = \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{1/3}(f)$.
nodes.name: Approximate degree (bounded outside the promise)
nodes.statement_short: Least degree of a polynomial that $\varepsilon$-approximates $f$ on the promise and stays bounded by $1+\varepsilon$ off it.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations

nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \{-1,1\}^n$, and let $f : \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\}$. Then $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(f) \geq d$ if and only if there exists a function $\psi \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the following properties. \begin{align} &\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\psi(x) \cdot f(x) - \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n \setminus \mathcal{X}} |\psi(x)| > \varepsilon, \\ &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} |\psi(x)| = 1, \text{ and } \\ &\text{ For every polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R} \text{ of degree less than } d, \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0. \end{align}

nodes.statement_short: $\widetilde{\deg}_\varepsilon(f)\ge d$ iff a dual polynomial with correlation $>\varepsilon$, unit $\ell_1$-norm and pure high degree $d$ exists.

nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\mathcal{X}$ be a finite set. The $\varepsilon$-\emph{unbounded approximate degree} of a Boolean function $f : \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\}$, denoted $\widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_\varepsilon(f)$, is the least degree of a real polynomial $p : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $|p(x) - f(x)| \le \varepsilon$ for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$ (if $\mathcal{X}$ is a strict subset of a larger domain, then no constraints are placed on $p(x)$ for $x \not\in \mathcal{X}$). We use the term \emph{unbounded approximate degree} without qualification to refer to $\widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}(f) = \widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_{1/3}(f)$.
nodes.name: Unbounded approximate degree
nodes.statement_short: Least degree of a polynomial that $\varepsilon$-approximates $f$ on the promise, with no constraint outside it.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations

Then $\widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_{\varepsilon}(f) \geq d$ if and only if there exists a function $\psi \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the following properties. \begin{align} &\psi(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in \mathcal{X}, \\ &\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\psi(x) \cdot f(x) > \varepsilon, \\ &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} |\psi(x)| = 1, \text{ and } \\ &\text{ For every polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R} \text{ of degree less than } d, \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0. \end{align}

nodes.statement: Let $p \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \{-1,1\}$ be an arbitrary polynomial and let $[n]_0$ denote the set $\{0, 1, \dots, n\}$. Then there is a univariate polynomial $q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ of degree at most $\deg(p)$ such that \[q(t) = \frac{1}{\binom{n}{ t}} \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n \colon |x|=t} p(x)\] for all $t \in [n]_0$.
nodes.name: Minsky-Papert symmetrization
conclusions: there is a univariate polynomial $q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ of degree at most $\deg(p)$ such that \[q(t) = \frac{1}{\binom{n}{ t}} \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n \colon |x|=t} p(x)\] for all $t \in [n]_0$
nodes.label: lem:mp

nodes.statement: For $N \ge R$, we define $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R} : [R]^N \to \{-1,1\}$ by $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff for every $j \in [R]$, there exists an $i$ such that $s_i = j$.
nodes.name: Surjectivity function
nodes.label: def:surj

nodes.statement: For $N \ge R$, we define $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R} : [R]_0^N \to \{-1,1\}$ by $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff for every $j \in [R]$, there exists an $i$ such that $s_i = j$.
nodes.name: Surjectivity with a dummy element
nodes.label: def:dumsurj

nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $N \ge R$. Then \[ \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}) \le \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R + 1}) \cdot \log(R+1).\]
nodes.name: Reduction from dSURJ to SURJ
conclusions: \[ \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}) \le \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R + 1}) \cdot \log(R+1).\]
nodes.label: prop:dumsurj-reduction

nodes.statement: Let $p : \{-1,1\}^{(N+1) \cdot \log(R+1)} \to \{-1,1\}$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R+1}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$. Recall that an input to $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$ takes the form $(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ where each $s_i$ is the binary representation of a number in $[R]_0$. Define the transformation $T : [R]_0 \to [R + 1]$ by \[T(s) = \begin{cases} R + 1 & \text{ if } s = 0 \\ s & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\] Note that as a mapping between binary representations, the function $T$ is exactly computed by a vector of polynomials of degree at most $\log(R+1)$. For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R+1}(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1).\] Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1)\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Map the dummy element 0 to a fresh range item $R+1$ and append $R+1$, then compose an approximation for $\mathsf{SURJ}_{N+1,R+1}$ with this low-degree transformation.

nodes.name: Take an approximation p for SURJ
nodes.statement: Let $p : \{-1,1\}^{(N+1) \cdot \log(R+1)} \to \{-1,1\}$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R+1}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix an approximating polynomial $p$ for $\mathsf{SURJ}_{N+1,R+1}$.

nodes.name: Input encoding
nodes.statement: Recall that an input to $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$ takes the form $(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ where each $s_i$ is the binary representation of a number in $[R]_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the binary encoding of inputs.

nodes.name: Transformation T
nodes.statement: Define the transformation $T : [R]_0 \to [R + 1]$ by \[T(s) = \begin{cases} R + 1 & \text{ if } s = 0 \\ s & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\] Note that as a mapping between binary representations, the function $T$ is exactly computed by a vector of polynomials of degree at most $\log(R+1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $T$ sending the dummy 0 to $R+1$; it has low degree.

nodes.name: dSURJ as SURJ of transformed input
nodes.statement: For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R+1}(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1).\]
nodes.statement_short: dSURJ equals SURJ on the transformed input with $R+1$ appended.

nodes.name: Compose
nodes.statement: Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1)\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose $p$ with $T$ to approximate dSURJ.

nodes.statement: For integers $k, N, R$ with $k \le N$, define the function $\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R} : [R]^N \to \{-1,1\}$ by $\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff there exist $r \in [R]$ and distinct indices $i_1, \dots, i_k$ such that $s_{i_1} = \dots = s_{i_k} = r$.
nodes.name: k-distinctness function

nodes.statement: For integers $k, N, R$ with $k \le N$, define the function $\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R} : [R]_0^N \to \{-1,1\}$ by $\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff there exist $r \in [R]$ and distinct indices $i_1, \dots, i_k$ such that $s_{i_1} = \dots = s_{i_k} = r$.
nodes.name: k-distinctness with a dummy element

nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$, $N, R \in \mathbb{N}$, and $k \ge 2$. Then \[ \deg_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}) \le \deg_\varepsilon(\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}) \cdot \log(R+1).\]
nodes.name: Reduction from dDIST to DIST
conclusions: \[ \deg_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}) \le \deg_\varepsilon(\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}) \cdot \log(R+1).\]
nodes.label: prop:dumdist-reduction

nodes.statement: The proof is similar to that of \Cref{prop:dumsurj-reduction}, but uses a slightly more involved reduction. Let $p : \{-1,1\}^{2N\cdot \log(R+N)} \to \{-1,1\}$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}$. For each $i = 1, \dots, R$, define a transformation $T_i : [R]_0 \to [R+N]$ by \[T_i(s) = \begin{cases} R + i & \text{ if } s = 0 \\ s & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\] As a mapping between binary representations, the function $T=(T_1, \dots, T_N)$ is exactly computed by a vector of polynomials of degree at most $\log(R+1)$. For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}(T_1(s_1), \dots, T_N(s_N)).\] Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N))\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: As for dSURJ: send each dummy occurrence to a distinct fresh range item and compose with an approximation for $\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N,R+N}$.

nodes.name: Similar to dSURJ
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to that of \Cref{prop:dumsurj-reduction}, but uses a slightly more involved reduction.
nodes.statement_short: Same approach as the dSURJ reduction.

nodes.name: Take an approximation p for DIST
nodes.statement: Let $p : \{-1,1\}^{2N\cdot \log(R+N)} \to \{-1,1\}$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix an approximating polynomial $p$ for $\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N,R+N}$.

nodes.name: Transformations T_i
nodes.statement: For each $i = 1, \dots, R$, define a transformation $T_i : [R]_0 \to [R+N]$ by \[T_i(s) = \begin{cases} R + i & \text{ if } s = 0 \\ s & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\] As a mapping between binary representations, the function $T=(T_1, \dots, T_N)$ is exactly computed by a vector of polynomials of degree at most $\log(R+1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Map each dummy occurrence to a distinct fresh item.

nodes.name: dDIST as DIST of transformed input
nodes.statement: For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}(T_1(s_1), \dots, T_N(s_N)).\]
nodes.statement_short: dDIST equals DIST on the transformed input.

nodes.name: Compose
nodes.statement: Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N))\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose $p$ with $T$.

nodes.statement: For functions $f : Y^n \to Z$ and $g: X \to Y$, define the \emph{block composition} $f \circ g : X^n \to Z$ by $(f\circ g)(x_1, \dots, x_n) = f(g(x_1), \dots, g(x_n))$, for all $x_1, \dots, x_n \in X$.
nodes.name: Block composition
also_stated_at: Here, a function $g \colon \{-1,1\}^{n \cdot m} \to \{-1,1\}$ is the block-composition of $h \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \{-1,1\}$ and $f \colon \{-1,1\}^m \to \{-1,1\}$ if $g$ interprets its input as a sequence of $n$ blocks, applies $f$ to each block, and then feeds the $n$ outputs into $h$.
nodes.section: 2.5 Connecting Symmetric Properties and Block Composed Functions

nodes.statement: Suppose $g$ is a \emph{symmetric} function, in the sense that for any $x \in \{-1,1\}^N$ and any permutation $\sigma : [N] \to [N]$, we have \[g(x_1, \dots, x_N) = g(x_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(N)}).\]
nodes.name: Symmetric function
nodes.section: 2.5 Connecting Symmetric Properties and Block Composed Functions

nodes.statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ give rise to two functions. The first, which we denote by $F^{\operatorname{prop}} : [R]_0^N \to \{-1,1\}$, is a certain property of a list of numbers $s_1, \dots, s_N \in [R]_0$. The second, which we denote by $F^{\le N} : H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R} \to \{-1,1\}$, is the block composition of $f$ and $g$ restricted to inputs of Hamming weight at most $N$. Formally, these functions are defined as: \begin{align*} &F^{\operatorname{prop}}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = f(g({\mathds{1}}[s_1 = 1], \dots, {\mathds{1}}[s_N = 1]), \dots, g({\mathds{1}}[s_1=R], \dots,{\mathds{1}}[s_N=R])) \\ &F^{\le N}(x_1, \dots, x_R) = \begin{cases} f(g(x_1), \dots, g(x_R)) & \text{ if } x_1, \dots, x_R \in \{-1,1\}^N, |x_1| + \dots + |x_R| \le N.\\ \text{undefined} & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{align*}
nodes.name: F^prop and F^{<=N}
nodes.statement_short: $F^{\mathrm{prop}}$ applies $f\circ g$ to the indicator vectors of the range items; $F^{\le N}$ is $f\circ g$ restricted to total Hamming weight $\le N$.
nodes.section: 2.5 Connecting Symmetric Properties and Block Composed Functions

nodes.statement: Let $f : \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ be any function and let $g : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be a symmetric function. Then for $F^{\operatorname{prop}}$ and $F^{\le N}$ defined above, and for any $\varepsilon > 0$, we have \[\deg_\varepsilon(F^{\operatorname{prop}}) \ge \widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_\varepsilon(F^{\le N}).\]
nodes.name: Symmetric property vs. block composition reduction
nodes.origin_citation: Bun and Thaler (adegsurj), building on Ambainis
nodes.statement_short: The approximate degree of a symmetric property $F^{\mathrm{prop}}$ is at least the unbounded approximate degree of the weight-restricted block composition $F^{\le N}$.
conclusions: \[\deg_\varepsilon(F^{\operatorname{prop}}) \ge \widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_\varepsilon(F^{\le N}).\]
nodes.section: 2.5 Connecting Symmetric Properties and Block Composed Functions
nodes.label: thm:main-reduction

nodes.statement: In the case where $f = \mathsf{AND}_R$ and $g = \mathsf{ OR}_N$, the function $F^{\operatorname{prop}}(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ is the Surjectivity function augmented with a dummy item, $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N)$.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate the symmetric-property reduction with $f=\mathsf{AND}_R$, $g=\mathsf{OR}_N$.
nodes.section: 2.5 Connecting Symmetric Properties and Block Composed Functions

nodes.statement: Let $N, R \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}) \ge \widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_\varepsilon(F^{\le N})\] where $F^{\le N} : H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N} \to \{-1,1\}$ is the restriction of $\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ to $H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N}$.
nodes.name: Surjectivity reduces to promise AND-OR
conclusions: \[\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}) \ge \widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_\varepsilon(F^{\le N})\] where $F^{\le N} : H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N} \to \{-1,1\}$ is the restriction of $\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ to $H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N}$
nodes.section: 2.5 Connecting Symmetric Properties and Block Composed Functions
nodes.label: cor:surj-reduction

nodes.statement: For integers $k, N$ with $k \le N$, define the function $\mathsf{THR}^k_N : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ by $\mathsf{THR}^k_N(x) = -1$ iff $|x| \ge k$.
nodes.name: Threshold function THR
also_stated_at: Here $\mathsf{THR}^k_N \colon \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ denotes the function that evaluates to $-1$ if and only if the Hamming weight of its input is at least $k$.
nodes.section: 2.5 Connecting Symmetric Properties and Block Composed Functions

nodes.statement: If we let $f = \mathsf{ OR}_R$ and $g = \mathsf{THR}_N^k$, then the function $F^{\operatorname{prop}}$ is the dummy augmented $k$-distinctness function $\mathsf{dDIST}_{N, R}^k$.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate the symmetric-property reduction with $f=\mathsf{OR}_R$, $g=\mathsf{THR}^k_N$.
nodes.section: 2.5 Connecting Symmetric Properties and Block Composed Functions

nodes.statement: Let $N, R \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}) \ge \widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_\varepsilon(G^{\le N})\] where $G^{\le N} : H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N} \to \{-1,1\}$ is the restriction of $\mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N$ to $H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N}$.
nodes.name: k-distinctness reduces to promise OR-THR
conclusions: \[\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}) \ge \widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_\varepsilon(G^{\le N})\] where $G^{\le N} : H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N} \to \{-1,1\}$ is the restriction of $\mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N$ to $H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N}$
nodes.section: 2.5 Connecting Symmetric Properties and Block Composed Functions
nodes.label: cor:dist-reduction

nodes.statement: Let $\Psi : \{-1,1\}^M \to \mathbb{R}$ and $\psi : \{-1,1\}^m \to \mathbb{R}$ be functions that are not identically zero. Let $x=(x_1, \dots, x_M) \in \left(\{-1,1\}^{m}\right)^M$. Define the \emph{dual block composition} of $\Psi$ and $\psi$, denoted $\Psi \star \psi : (\{-1,1\}^m)^M \to \mathbb{R}$, by \[(\Psi \star \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M) = 2^M \cdot \Psi(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}\left(\psi(x_i)\right), \dots) \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^M |\psi(x_i)|.\]
nodes.name: Dual block composition
nodes.statement_short: $\Psi\star\psi$ evaluates $\Psi$ on the signs of $\psi$ on each block, weighted by the product of $|\psi|$ values.

nodes.statement: The dual block composition satisfies the following properties: \paragraph{\emph{Preservation of $\ell_1$-norm}:} If $\|\Psi\|_1 = 1$, $\|\psi\|_1 = 1$, and $\langle \psi, \mathbf{1}\rangle = 0$, then \begin{equation}\|\Psi \star \psi\|_1 = 1. \end{equation} \paragraph{\emph{Multiplicativity of pure high degree}:} If $\langle \Psi, P \rangle = 0$ for every polynomial $P \colon \{-1,1\}^M \to \{-1,1\}$ of degree less than $D$, and $\langle \psi, p \rangle = 0$ for every polynomial $p \colon \{-1,1\}^m \to \{-1,1\}$ of degree less than $d$, then for every polynomial $q \colon \{-1,1\}^{m \cdot M} \to \{-1,1\}$, \begin{equation}\deg q < D \cdot d \implies \langle \Psi \star \psi, q \rangle = 0. \end{equation} \paragraph{\emph{Associativity}:} For every $\zeta: \{-1,1\}^{m_\zeta} \to \mathbb{R}$, $\varphi: \{-1,1\}^{m_\varphi} \to \mathbb{R}$, and $\psi: \{-1,1\}^{m_\psi} \to \mathbb{R}$, we have \begin{equation} (\zeta \star \varphi) \star \psi = \zeta \star (\varphi \star \psi). \end{equation}
nodes.name: Properties of dual block composition
nodes.statement_short: Dual block composition preserves $\ell_1$-norm, multiplies pure high degree, and is associative.

conclusions: \begin{equation}\|\Psi \star \psi\|_1 = 1. \end{equation}

nodes.statement: Let $M \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha, \beta > 0$. A function $\omega: [M]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the $(\alpha, \beta)$-decay condition if \begin{align} &\sum_{t = 0}^M \omega(t) = 0, \\ &\sum_{t = 0}^M |\omega(t)| = 1, \\ &|\omega(t)| \le \alpha \exp (-\beta t) / t^2 \quad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, M. \end{align}
nodes.name: (alpha, beta)-decay condition
nodes.statement_short: A balanced, unit-$\ell_1$ function on $[M]_0$ whose $t$-th value decays like $\alpha e^{-\beta t}/t^2$.

nodes.statement: Let $R \in \mathbb{N}$ be sufficiently large, and let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\Phi\|_1 = 1$. For $M \le R$, let $\omega : [M]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the $(\alpha, \beta)$-decay condition with parameters $1 \leq \alpha \le R^2, \beta \in (4\ln^2 R/ \sqrt{\alpha} R, 1)$. Let $N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R$, and define $\psi: \{-1,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\psi(x) = \omega(|x|) / \binom{N}{|x|}$. If $D < N$ is such that \begin{equation} \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ with } \deg p < D, \text{ we have } \langle \Phi \star \psi, p \rangle = 0, \end{equation} then there exist $\Delta \ge \beta\sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R$ and a function $\zeta: (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align}& \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ with } \deg p < \min\{D, \Delta\}, \text{ we have } \langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0, \\ &\|\zeta - \Phi \star \psi\|_1 \le \frac{2}{9}, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ &\zeta \text{ is supported on } H^{N \cdot R}_{\le N}. \end{align}
nodes.name: Zeroing out high-Hamming-weight mass
nodes.statement_short: If $\omega$ satisfies the decay condition and $N=\Theta(\sqrt{\alpha}R)$, $\Phi\star\psi$ can be corrected to a unit-norm dual supported on weight $\le N$ with pure high degree $\min\{D,\Delta\}$.

nodes.statement: To control this quantity, we appeal to the following combinatorial lemma, whose proof we delay to \Cref{s:proofofcomb} (this lemma is a substantial refinement of \cite[Lemma 32]{adegsurj}). \begin{restatable}{lemma}{combinatorial} Let $\alpha \le R^2$, let $\beta \in (4\ln^2 R/ \sqrt{\alpha} R, 1)$, and let $R$ be sufficiently large. Let $N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha}\rceil R$. Let $\eta_i :[M]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, for $i = 1, \dots R$, be a sequence of non-negative functions where for every $i$, \begin{align}&\sum_{r = 0}^M \eta_i(r) \le 1 / 2 \\ &\eta_i(r) \le \alpha \exp(-\beta r) / r^2 \qquad \forall r = 1, \dots, M. \end{align} Let $P = \{\vec{t} = (t_1, \dots, t_R) \in [M]_0^R : t_1 + \dots + t_R > N\}$. Then \[\sum_{\vec{t} \in P} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) \le 2^{-R} \cdot (2NR)^{-2\Delta}\] where $\Delta \ge \beta\sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R$. \end{restatable}

nodes.statement: \Cref{prop:correction} is framed exclusively in the language of dual polynomials: it states that if a dual polynomial $\xi$ places very little mass on inputs of Hamming weight more than $N$, then there exists another dual polynomial $\nu$ satisfying certain useful properties (we ultimately use $\nu$ to zero out the mass that $\xi$ places on inputs of Hamming weight more than $N$). \Cref{prop:correction} also has a clean \emph{primal} formulation. Roughly speaking, it is equivalent to a bound on the growth rate of any polynomial of degree at most $D$ that is bounded at all inputs of Hamming weight at most $D$. We direct the interested reader to \cite{violalecturenotes} for details of this primal formulation.

nodes.statement: Let $T = \lfloor \frac{N}{2M} \rfloor$. For each $s \in \{T, \dots, R\}$, let \[C(s) = \max \left\{ \frac{N}{6 s \ln R}, \frac{N}{6\sqrt{R \cdot s}} \right\}.\] We begin with a simple, but important, structural observation about the set $P$. Let $t = (t_1, \dots, t_R) \in [M]_0^R$ be a sequence such that $t_1 + \dots + t_R > N$. Then we claim that there exists an $s \in \{T \dots, R\}$ such that $t_i \ge C(s)$ for at least $s$ indices $i \in [R]$. To see this, assume without loss of generality that the entries of $\vec{t}$ are sorted so that $t_1 \ge t_2 \ge \dots \ge t_R$. Then there must exist an $s \geq T$ such that $t_s \ge C(s)$. Otherwise, because no $t_i$ can exceed $M$, we would have: \begin{align*} t_1 + \dots + t_R &< T \cdot M + \sum_{s = 1}^R C(s) \\ &\le \frac{N}{2} + \frac{N}{6 \ln R} \sum_{s = 1}^{\lfloor R / \ln^2 R \rfloor} \frac{1}{s} + \frac{N}{6\sqrt{R}} \sum_{s = \lceil R / \ln^2 R \rceil}^R \frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}\\ &\le \frac{N}{2}+ \frac{N}{6} + \frac{N}{3} \\ &= N. \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from \Cref{lem:inv-sqrt} and the fact that $\sum_{s = 1}^m s^{-1} \le \ln m + 1$ (and $R$ is sufficiently large). Since the entries of $\vec{t}$ are sorted, the preceding values $t_1, \dots, t_{s-1} \geq C(s)$ as well. For each subset $S \subseteq [R]$, define \[P_S = \{\vec{t} \in P : t_i \ge C(|S|)\text{ for all indices }i \in S\}.\] The observations above guarantee that for every $\vec{t}=(t_1, \dots, t_R) \in P$, there exists some set $S$ of size at least $s \in \{T, \dots, R\}$ such that $t_i \geq C(s)$ for all $i \in S$. Hence \begin{align*} \hspace{-10mm} \sum_{\vec{t} \in P} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) & \leq \sum_{s = T}^{R} \sum_{S \subseteq [R] : |S| = s} \sum_{\vec{t} \in P_S} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) \\ & \leq \sum_{s = T}^{R} \binom{R}{s} \left( \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, R\}} \left( \sum_{r=\lceil C(s) \rceil}^M \eta_i(r)\right) \right)^s \left( \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, R\}} \left( \sum_{r = 0}^M \eta_i(r) \right)\right)^{R-s} \hspace{-3.3em}&\hspace{-3em}\\ &\leq 2^{-R}\sum_{s = T}^{R} \binom{R}{s} \left( \sum_{r = \lceil C(s) \rceil}^M 2\alpha \exp(-\beta r ) r^{-2} \right)^s & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by Properties } \eqref{eqn:eta-bound} \text{ and } \eqref{eqn:eta-decay}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{2\alpha}{(C(s))^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \sum_{r = \lceil C(s) \rceil}^\infty \exp\left(-\beta r s\right) & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by \Cref{lem:binomial}}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{2\alpha}{(C(s))^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\beta s}} \cdot \exp\left(-\beta s C(s)\right) & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by \Cref{lem:inv-exp-tail}}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{72\alpha R s}{N^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \frac{2}{\beta} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\beta N}{6\ln R}\right) & \text{by definition of $C(s)$}\\ &\qquad\qquad\text{ and since } \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\beta s}} \le \frac{1}{1 - (1-\beta/2)} = \frac{2}{\beta} \text{ for } s \ge 1, \beta \in (0, 1) \hspace{-10em}&\hspace{-10em} \\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} 2^{-s} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{3 \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R }{ \ln R} + \ln(2/\beta)\right)&\hspace{-28mm}\text{setting } N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha}\rceil R \\ &\le 2^{-R} \cdot (2 N R)^{-2\Delta}, \end{align*} where \[\Delta = \frac{1}{2\ln(2NR)} \cdot \left(\frac{3\beta \sqrt{\alpha} R}{\ln R} - \ln(2/\beta) \right) \ge \frac{\beta \sqrt{\alpha} R}{4\ln^2 R}\] holds for sufficiently large $R$ by the restrictions placed on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in the statement of the lemma.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Every tuple with large sum has $s$ coordinates above $C(s)$; union bound over such sets with the binomial and geometric-tail lemmas.

nodes.name: Union bound
nodes.statement: The observations above guarantee that for every $\vec{t}=(t_1, \dots, t_R) \in P$, there exists some set $S$ of size at least $s \in \{T, \dots, R\}$ such that $t_i \geq C(s)$ for all $i \in S$. Hence \begin{align*} \hspace{-10mm} \sum_{\vec{t} \in P} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) & \leq \sum_{s = T}^{R} \sum_{S \subseteq [R] : |S| = s} \sum_{\vec{t} \in P_S} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) \\ & \leq \sum_{s = T}^{R} \binom{R}{s} \left( \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, R\}} \left( \sum_{r=\lceil C(s) \rceil}^M \eta_i(r)\right) \right)^s \left( \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, R\}} \left( \sum_{r = 0}^M \eta_i(r) \right)\right)^{R-s} \hspace{-3.3em}&\hspace{-3em}\\ &\leq 2^{-R}\sum_{s = T}^{R} \binom{R}{s} \left( \sum_{r = \lceil C(s) \rceil}^M 2\alpha \exp(-\beta r ) r^{-2} \right)^s & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by Properties } \eqref{eqn:eta-bound} \text{ and } \eqref{eqn:eta-decay}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{2\alpha}{(C(s))^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \sum_{r = \lceil C(s) \rceil}^\infty \exp\left(-\beta r s\right) & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by \Cref{lem:binomial}}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{2\alpha}{(C(s))^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\beta s}} \cdot \exp\left(-\beta s C(s)\right) & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by \Cref{lem:inv-exp-tail}}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{72\alpha R s}{N^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \frac{2}{\beta} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\beta N}{6\ln R}\right) & \text{by definition of $C(s)$}\\ &\qquad\qquad\text{ and since } \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\beta s}} \le \frac{1}{1 - (1-\beta/2)} = \frac{2}{\beta} \text{ for } s \ge 1, \beta \in (0, 1) \hspace{-10em}&\hspace{-10em} \\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} 2^{-s} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{3 \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R }{ \ln R} + \ln(2/\beta)\right)&\hspace{-28mm}\text{setting } N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha}\rceil R \\ &\le 2^{-R} \cdot (2 N R)^{-2\Delta}, \end{align*} where \[\Delta = \frac{1}{2\ln(2NR)} \cdot \left(\frac{3\beta \sqrt{\alpha} R}{\ln R} - \ln(2/\beta) \right) \ge \frac{\beta \sqrt{\alpha} R}{4\ln^2 R}\] holds for sufficiently large $R$ by the restrictions placed on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in the statement of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over $S$ using the binomial and geometric-tail lemmas.

nodes.statement: For any $R \in \mathbb{N}$, we have $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N,R}) = \tilde{O}(N^{3/4})$.

nodes.statement: For the remainder of the section, we focus on proving \Cref{thm:upper} in the case that $R=\Theta(N)$. This is without loss of generality by the following argument. If $R > N$, then Surjectivity\ is identically false, and hence has (exact) degree 0. And if $R=o(N)$, then we can reduce to the case $R=\Theta(N)$ as follows. Let $N'=2N$ and $R' = R + N$; clearly $R' = \Theta(N)$. Given an input $x$ to $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}$, obtain an input $x'$ to $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N', R'}$ by appending range elements $R+1, \dots, R+N$ to $x$. This construction guarantees that $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}(x) = \mathsf{ SURJ}_{N', R'}(x')$. It follows that an approximation of degree $\tilde{O}(N^{3/4})$ for $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N', R'}$ implies an approximation of the same degree for $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.name: Proof (reduction to R = Theta(N))
nodes.statement_short: Without loss of generality $R=\Theta(N)$: trivial if $R>N$, and pad the input with fresh range items if $R=o(N)$.

nodes.statement: \caption{An informal description of the polynomial approximation for $\mathsf{ NOR}$} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \vspace{0.25em} \State Using $q$, check if $|x|>T$ (with exponentially small probability of error if indeed $|x| > T$). nodes.statement: To establish property (1), we use the fact that for $\mu > 0$, the value of the degree $d$ Chebyshev polynomial can be written~\cite[\S 3.2 Problem 8(f)]{cheney} as \begin{align*} T_d(1 + \mu) &= \cosh ( d \operatorname{arcosh} ( 1 + \mu) ) \\ & \ge \cosh ( d \sqrt{\mu} ) & \text{ for } \mu \le 1\\ & \ge \frac{1}{2} \cdot \exp(d \sqrt{\mu}). \end{align*} Property (2) appears as~\cite[3.2 Problem 19]{cheney}.

nodes.statement: Choose $d = O(\sqrt{T} \log(1/\varepsilon))$ so that $M := T_d(1 + 1/T) + 1\ge 2/\varepsilon$ (as guaranteed by Property 1 of \Cref{lem:cheb}). Define $V_{T, \varepsilon}$ by the following affine transformation of $T_d$: \[V_{T, \varepsilon}(x) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T} - \frac{|x|}{T}\right).\] Then for $|x| = 0$, we have \[V_{T, \varepsilon}(x) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T}\right) = 0.\] If $1 \le |x| \le T$, then $1 + 1/T - |x| / T \in [-1, 1]$, so $V_{T, \varepsilon(x)} \in [1-\varepsilon, 1]$. Finally, if $T +1 \le |x| \le N$, then \[|V_{T, \varepsilon}(x)| \le 1 + \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d(N / T) \le \exp(O(\sqrt{T} \cdot\log N \cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)),\] where the final inequality holds by Equation \eqref{eq:swell}.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Affine transformation of the Chebyshev polynomial $T_d$ evaluated at $1+1/T-|x|/T$; case analysis on $|x|$.

nodes.statement: Let $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ and $g : X \to \{0,1\}$ be Boolean functions, where $X \subseteq \{0, 1\}^m$ for some $m$. Let $p : \{0,1\}^n \to [0, 1]$ be an $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $f$, and let $q : X \to [0, 1]$ be a $\delta$-approximating polynomial for $g$. Then the block composition $p \circ q : X^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is an $(\varepsilon + \delta n)$-approximating polynomial for $f \circ g : X^n \to \{0,1\}$.
nodes.name: Composition of approximating polynomials
assumptions: $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ and $g : X \to \{0,1\}$ be Boolean functions, where $X \subseteq \{0, 1\}^m$ for some $m$
conclusions: the block composition $p \circ q : X^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is an $(\varepsilon + \delta n)$-approximating polynomial for $f \circ g : X^n \to \{0,1\}$

nodes.label: lem:naive

nodes.statement: Fix any input $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in X^n$, and let $y = (g(x_1), \dots, g(x_n)) \in \{0,1\}^n$. Let $z \in [0, 1]^n$ be defined by $z = (q(x_1), \dots, q(x_n))$. Since $p$ is an $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $f$, by the triangle inequality, it suffices to show that $|p(y) - p(z)| \le \delta n$. Let $Z$ be a random variable on $\{0,1\}^n$ where each $Z_i = 1$ independently with probability $z_i$. Then due to the multilinearity of $p$, we have \[p(z) = \mathbb{E}[p(Z)] = \Pr[Z =y] \cdot p(y) + \Pr[Z \ne y] \cdot \mathbb{E}[p(Z) | Z \ne y].\] Since $q$ is a $\delta$-approximating polynomial for $g$, we have $|y_i - z_i| \le \delta$ for every $i \in [n]$. Hence, \[\Pr[Z = y] \ge \left(1 - \delta \right)^n \ge 1 - \delta n.\] Because $p$ is bounded in $[0, 1]$, this implies \[p(z) \ge (1 - \delta n) \cdot p(y) + 0 \ge p(y) - \delta n\] and \[p(z) \le 1 \cdot p(y) + \delta n \cdot 1 = p(y) + \delta n,\] completing the proof.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Probabilistic argument: view $p(z)$ as the expectation of $p$ on a random input that equals $y$ with probability $\ge 1-\delta n$.
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Because $p$ is bounded in $[0, 1]$, this implies \[p(z) \ge (1 - \delta n) \cdot p(y) + 0 \ge p(y) - \delta n\] and \[p(z) \le 1 \cdot p(y) + \delta n \cdot 1 = p(y) + \delta n,\] completing the proof.

nodes.statement: We prove the lemma by induction on the number of variables $n$. If $n = 0$, then $p$ is a constant in the interval $[0, 1]$ and the claim is true. Now suppose the claim is true for $n-1$ variables, and let $p : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ with $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for $x \in \{0,1\}^n$. We begin by decomposing \[p(x) = (1-x_n) \cdot q_0(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}) + x_n \cdot q_1(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})\] where $q_0$ and $q_1$ are themselves multilinear polynomials. Since $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for all $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, this is in particular true when $x_n = 0$. Hence $q_0(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \{0,1\}^{n-1}$. Similarly, setting $x_n = 1$ reveals that $q_1(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \{0,1\}^{n-1}$. Now for any $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $x' = (x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})$ we have \begin{align*} |p(x)| &= \left| (1 - x_n) \cdot q_0(x') + x_n \cdot q_1(x')\right| \\ &\le |1 - x_n| \cdot |q_0(x')| + |x_n| \cdot |q_1(x')| \\ &\le (|1 - x_n| + |x_n|) \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^{n-1} (|1 - x_i| + |x_i|) \end{align*} where the final inequality uses the inductive hypothesis. This proves the claim.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the number of variables, decomposing $p$ along the last variable.

nodes.statement: The first two cases are an immediate consequence of \Cref{approxlemma}. To upper bound the value of $|p_{\mathcal{R}}(x)|$ for $x\notin \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{R}}$, we exploit the structure of $p_{\mathcal{R}}$ as a multilinear polynomial $w$ of degree $O(\sqrt{N})$ over the variables $z_1,\ldots,z_{|\mathcal{R}|}$, where each $z_r$ is the output of the $r^\mathrm{th}$ polynomial from \Cref{lem:orT}. That is, $$z_r = V_{T, 1/(20n)}\left({\mathds{1}}[x_1 = r], \dots, {\mathds{1}}[x_N = r]\right).$$ If $b_{\mathcal{R}}(x)$ range items appear greater than $T$ times, this means that up to $b_{\mathcal{R}}(x)$ of the variables $z_r$ might take values outside $[0,1]$. However, by \Cref{lem:orT}, each of these $b_{\mathcal{R}}(x)$ variables is still at most ${\exp(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}))}$. By \Cref{lem:real-bound}, \[|w(z)| \le \prod_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \left(|1 - z_r| + |z_r|\right) \le \exp\left(b_{\mathcal{R}}(x) \cdot \tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right),\] since each $z_r $ that is in $[0, 1]$ contributes a factor of exactly $1$ to the product, whereas each of the remaining $b_{\mathcal{R}}(x)$ variables contributes a factor of at most ${\exp(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}))}$ to the product.

nodes.statement: \caption{Informal description of the polynomial approximation for $\mathsf{ SURJ}$} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \vspace{0.25em} \State Sample $S=\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4})$ items and remove all range items seen from $[R]$. Let the remaining set be $\mathcal{R} \subseteq [R]$. \State Solve $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{\mathcal{R}}$ under the promise that all $r\in\mathcal{R}$ have $\operatorname{\#}_r(x)\leq T$, where $T=\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N})$. \end{algorithmic}
nodes.name: Informal polynomial approximation for SURJ
nodes.statement_short: Sample $\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4})$ items to discard frequent range items, then solve $\mathsf{SURJ}_{\mathcal{R}}$ on the remaining low-frequency items.
nodes.label: alg:SURJalmost

nodes.name: Sample and discard seen range items
nodes.statement: Sample $S=\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4})$ items and remove all range items seen from $[R]$. Let the remaining set be $\mathcal{R} \subseteq [R]$.

nodes.name: Solve SURJ_R on remaining items
nodes.statement: Solve $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{\mathcal{R}}$ under the promise that all $r\in\mathcal{R}$ have $\operatorname{\#}_r(x)\leq T$, where $T=\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N})$.

nodes.statement: If we denote the input $x\in[R]^N$ restricted to the subset $\mathcal{S} \subseteq [N]$ as $x_{\mathcal{S}}$, then this algorithm outputs $1$ if and only if $x_{\mathcal{S}} = y$.

nodes.statement: \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{y \in [R]^S} {\mathds{1}}_y(x_{\mathcal{S}}) f(\mathcal{S},y) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} f(\mathcal{S},x_{\mathcal{S}}).

nodes.statement: Specifically, if we sample the set $\mathcal{S} \subseteq [N]$, and learn that $x_{\mathcal{S}}$ equals the string $y\in[R]^{|\mathcal{S}|}$, then we want to run the polynomial $p_{\mathcal{R}}(y)$ from \Cref{lem:promiseSURJ} for the set $\mathcal{R}(y)$ of all elements in $[R]$ that do not appear in $y$, i.e., \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}(y) = [R] \setminus \{r:\exists i~y_i = r\}. \end{equation}
nodes.name: Unseen range items R(y)

nodes.statement: \mathcal{R}(y) = [R] \setminus \{r:\exists i~y_i = r\}.

nodes.label: nomoreeqs

nodes.name: Proof (construction of r(x))
nodes.statement_short: Average $p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}$ over random samples $\mathcal{S}$ of size $\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4})$. Samples leaving a frequent item unseen are exponentially rare, outweighing the growth of $p_{\mathcal{R}}$.

nodes.name: Define r(x)
nodes.statement: Using the tools from \Cref{sec:surj-hard-inputs} and the above discussion, we can now construct a polynomial that corresponds to the informal description in \Cref{alg:SURJalmost}: \begin{equation} r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{y \in [R]^S} {\mathds{1}}_y(x_{\mathcal{S}}) p_{\mathcal{R}(y)}(x). \end{equation} This is a polynomial of degree $S\log R + \max_{y}\{\deg(p_{\mathcal{R}(y)})\} = \tilde{O}(S + \sqrt{NT}) = \tilde{O}(N^{3/4})$, using $S=\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4})$ and $T=\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N})$ (where the factors hidden by the $\tilde{\Theta}$ notation will be chosen later). The value of the polynomial on input $x$ is \begin{equation} r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x). \end{equation} where recall that $\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})$ is as defined in Equation \eqref{nomoreeqs}. The right hand side of Equation \eqref{fleck} is precisely the expected value of the polynomial $p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)$ when $\mathcal{S}$ is a uniformly random set of size $S$. We will now show that $r(x)$ is an approximating polynomial for Surjectivity, i.e., that for all $x\in[R]^N$, $|\mathsf{ SURJ}(x)-r(x)|\leq 1/3$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $r(x)$ as the sample-average of $p_{\mathcal{R}(y)}$.

nodes.statement: r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{y \in [R]^S} {\mathds{1}}_y(x_{\mathcal{S}}) p_{\mathcal{R}(y)}(x).
nodes.name: Approximating polynomial r(x)

nodes.statement: r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x).
nodes.name: Value of r(x)
nodes.label: fleck

nodes.name: Split by b
nodes.statement: Recalling that $b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}$ is the number of range items $r \in \mathcal{R}$ that appear in $x$ greater than $T$ times (cf. Equation \eqref{eq:b}), we compute the value of the polynomial $r(x)$ on an input $x$: \begin{align} r(x) &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \\ &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \left(\sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{b=0}^{N/T} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=b] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \right)\\ &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=0] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad + \sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=b] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x), \end{align} where we split up the sum into the $b=0$ \eqref{eq:t1} and $b\geq 1$ \eqref{eq:t2} cases. We first show that the $b\geq1$ term \eqref{eq:t2} has essentially no contribution to the final value.
nodes.statement_short: Split by the number $b$ of frequent unseen items.

nodes.statement: r(x) &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \\ &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \left(\sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{b=0}^{N/T} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=b] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \right)\\ &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=0] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad + \sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=b] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x),

nodes.label: eq:t1

nodes.name: Bound b>=1 terms
nodes.statement: When $b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \geq 1$, we know by \Cref{lem:boundonprcal} that the magnitude of the polynomial $|p_{\mathcal{R}}(x)|$ is at most $\exp\left(b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \cdot \tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right)$. Thus the magnitude of the term in Expression \eqref{eq:t2} is at most \begin{align} &\sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=b] \cdot \exp(b \cdot \tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})) \\ =&\sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=b] \cdot \exp\left(b \cdot \tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the $b\ge1$ terms by the growth of $p_{\mathcal{R}}$.

nodes.statement: &\sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=b] \cdot \exp(b \cdot \tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})) \\ =&\sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=b] \cdot \exp\left(b \cdot \tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right).
nodes.name: Bound on the b>=1 term
Heuristic
nodes.statement: We now need to compute the value of $\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=b]$ for each $b$. Intuitively, this roughly corresponds to the probability that we sample $S=\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4})$ elements from the input and miss all $bT$ elements that correspond to the $T = \tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N})$ copies of the $b$ range items that appear at least $T$ times. If we were to sample $N / (bT)$ elements, the probability of seeing none of the $b T$ elements would be $\Theta(1)$. Since we are sampling $S=\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4}) \gg N / (bT)$ elements, the probability of not seeing one of the $bT$ elements is ${\exp(-bST/N)} = {\exp(-b \cdot \tilde{\Omega}(N^{1/4}))}$.
nodes.statement_short: Heuristic estimate of missing frequent items.

nodes.name: Missing-item lemma
nodes.statement_short: State and prove the missing-item lemma.

nodes.statement: Let $S, T \le N$. Let $\mathcal{S} \subset [N]$ be a random subset of size $S$. Then for every $x \in [R]^N$ and every $b \ge 1$, \[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \ge b] \leq {\exp(-b \cdot (ST/N - \log N))},\] recalling that $b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}$ is the number of range items $r \in \mathcal{R}$ that appear in $x$ more than $T$ times, but do not appear in $x_{\mathcal{S}}$.

conclusions: \[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \ge b] \leq {\exp(-b \cdot (ST/N - \log N))},\]

nodes.statement_short: Multiply the conditional probabilities.

nodes.name: Union bound
nodes.statement: Now fix an arbitrary $x$, and let $r_1, \dots, r_{k}$ be the range items appearing greater than $T$ times in $x$. Observe that $k \le N/T$. We estimate the probability of interest by taking a union bound over all subsets of $r_1, \dots, r_k$ of size $b$: \begin{align*} \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \ge b] &\le \sum_{Y \subseteq [k] : |Y| = b} \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_{i_j} \notin x_{\mathcal{S}} \quad \forall j \in Y] \\ & \le \binom{k}{b} \exp \left(-\frac{bST}{N}\right) \\ &\le \exp \left( -\frac{bST}{N} + b \log N\right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over $b$-subsets of frequent items.

nodes.name: b>=1 terms negligible
nodes.statement: From \Cref{lem:prob-b} we know that $\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=b] \leq {\exp(-b \cdot \tilde{\Omega}(ST/N))}$. Hence the $b\geq1$ term \eqref{eq:t2} is at most \begin{align} \sum_{b=1}^{N/T} {\exp(-b \cdot \tilde{\Omega}(ST/N))} \cdot {\exp(b \cdot \tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}))} = o(1), \end{align} by choosing $T = \tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N})$ and $S = \tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4})$ appropriately. This shows that the term in \eqref{eq:t2} does not significantly influence the value of the polynomial for any input $x$.
nodes.statement_short: The $b\ge1$ terms sum to $o(1)$.

nodes.statement: \sum_{b=1}^{N/T} {\exp(-b \cdot \tilde{\Omega}(ST/N))} \cdot {\exp(b \cdot \tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}))} = o(1),
nodes.name: Bound on the b>=1 term (formal)
r up to o(1)
nodes.statement: Thus we have for any input $x$, \begin{align} r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=0] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) + o(1). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $r(x)$ equals the $b=0$ term up to $o(1)$.

nodes.statement: r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=0] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) + o(1).
nodes.name: r(x) up to o(1)
Conclude
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lem:promiseSURJ}, we know that if $b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x)=0$ (and hence $x \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}$), then $p_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) $ is a $(1/10)$-approximation to $\mathsf{ SURJ}(x)$. Applying \Cref{lem:prob-b} once again shows that $\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) \ge 1] \le \exp(- \tilde{\Omega}(N^{1/4}))$, so $\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})}(x) = 0] = 1 - o(1)$. Hence, for all $x \in [R]^N$, $|r(x) - \mathsf{ SURJ}(x)| \le 1/10 + o(1) \le 1/3$. This completes the proof of \Cref{thm:upper}.
nodes.statement_short: The $b=0$ term approximates SURJ; error $\le 1/3$.

nodes.statement: For some $N = O(R)$, the $(1/3)$-approximate degree of $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}$ is $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4})$.
nodes.name: Approximate degree lower bound for Surjectivity
conclusions: the $(1/3)$-approximate degree of $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}$ is $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4})$
nodes.label: thm:surj

nodes.statement: Let $N = c \cdot R$ for a sufficiently large constant $c>0$. Let $F^{\le N} \colon H^{N \cdot R}_{\le N} \to \{-1,1\}$ equal $\mathsf{AND}_{R} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ restricted to inputs in $H^{N \cdot R}_{\le N} = \{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} : |x| \le N\}$. Then $\widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}(F^{\le N}) \ge \tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4}).$
nodes.name: Unbounded approximate degree of promise AND-OR
assumptions: $N = c \cdot R$ for a sufficiently large constant $c>0$
$F^{\le N} \colon H^{N \cdot R}_{\le N} \to \{-1,1\}$ equal $\mathsf{AND}_{R} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ restricted to inputs in $H^{N \cdot R}_{\le N} = \{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} : |x| \le N\}$
conclusions: $\widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}(F^{\le N}) \ge \tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4}).$
nodes.label: thm:main-amp

nodes.statement: Let $T \in \mathbb{N}$ and $1/T \le \delta \le 1/2$. There exist constants $c_1, c_2 \in (0, 1) $ and a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align} &\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^T \omega(t) \ge 1- \delta \\ &\sum_{t = 0}^T |\omega(t)| = 1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg q < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{170 \exp(-c_2 t \sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T})}{\delta \cdot t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, \dots, T.\end{align}
nodes.name: Univariate dual witness for OR with exponential decay
nodes.statement_short: There is a univariate dual for $\mathsf{OR}$ with correlation $1-\delta$, pure high degree $\Omega(\sqrt{\delta T})$ and tail decay $e^{-\Omega(t\sqrt{\delta/T})}/(\delta t^2)$.
conclusions: There exist constants $c_1, c_2 \in (0, 1) $ and a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align} &\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^T \omega(t) \ge 1- \delta \\ &\sum_{t = 0}^T |\omega(t)| = 1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg q < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{170 \exp(-c_2 t \sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T})}{\delta \cdot t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, \dots, T.\end{align}
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}
nodes.label: prop:or-sym-dual

nodes.statement: &\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^T \omega(t) \ge 1- \delta \\ &\sum_{t = 0}^T |\omega(t)| = 1

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Explicit construction: $\omega$ is a binomial-weighted product vanishing outside a sparse set $S$; pure high degree from the alternating binomial identity, then case analysis bounding $|\omega(t)|/\omega(0)$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Unnormalised goal
nodes.statement: By renormalizing, it suffices to construction a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align} &\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^T \omega(t) \ge (1 - \delta)\|\omega\|_1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg q < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{170 \exp(-c_2 t \sqrt{\delta} /\sqrt{T})\|\omega\|_1}{\delta \cdot t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, \dots, T.\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to unnormalised conditions.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.statement: &\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^T \omega(t) \ge (1 - \delta)\|\omega\|_1
nodes.name: Equation eqn:or-sym-corr-ref
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}
nodes.label: eqn:or-sym-corr-ref

nodes.statement: & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg q < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{170 \exp(-c_2 t \sqrt{\delta} /\sqrt{T})\|\omega\|_1}{\delta \cdot t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, \dots, T.
nodes.name: Equation eqn:or-sym-phd-ref, eqn:or-sym-decay-ref
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}
nodes.label: eqn:or-sym-phd-ref

nodes.name: Construct omega
nodes.statement: Let $c = \lceil 8 / \delta \rceil$ below. We will freely use the fact that since $\delta \le 1/2$, we have $c \le c^2 / (c-1) \le 10 /\delta$. Let $m = \lfloor \sqrt{T/2c} \rfloor$ and define the set \[S = \{1, c\} \cup \{2ci^2 : 0 \le i \le m\}.\] Note that $|S| \ge c_1 \sqrt{\delta T}$ for some absolute constant $c_1 > 0$. Define the function \[\omega(t) = \frac{(-1)^{t+(T-m)}}{T!} \binom{T}{t} \prod_{r \in [T]_0 \setminus S} (t - r).\]
nodes.statement_short: Define $c$, $m$, the set $S$ and $\omega$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Binomial identity
nodes.statement: Property~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-phd-ref} follows from the following well-known combinatorial identity. \begin{fact}[e.g., \cite{concrete} Equation (5.23) or \cite{osnewbounds}] Let $T \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $p$ be a polynomial of degree less than $T$. Then \[\sum_{t = 0}^T (-1)^t \binom{T}{t} p(t) = 0.\] \end{fact}
nodes.statement_short: Pure high degree from the alternating binomial identity.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.statement: Let $T \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $p$ be a polynomial of degree less than $T$. Then \[\sum_{t = 0}^T (-1)^t \binom{T}{t} p(t) = 0.\]
nodes.name: Alternating binomial sum identity
assumptions: $p$ be a polynomial of degree less than $T$
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}
nodes.label: fact:combinatorial

nodes.name: Formula for |omega|
nodes.statement: Expanding out the binomial coefficient in the definition of $\omega$ reveals that \[|\omega(t)| = \begin{cases} \prod\limits_{r \in S \setminus \{t\}} \frac{1}{|t - r|} & \text{ for } t \in S, \\ 0 & \text{ otherwise.} \end{cases}\]
nodes.statement_short: Closed form for $|\omega(t)|$ on $S$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Decay at t=1
nodes.statement: We now use this characterization to establish the improved tail decay property \eqref{eqn:or-sym-decay-ref}. This clearly holds for $t = 1$ with $c_2 = 1/10$, since $|\omega(1)| \le \|\omega\|_1$ and \[\frac{170}{\delta} \exp(-c_2\sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T}) \ge 340 \cdot e^{-\sqrt{2} / 10} > 1.\]
nodes.statement_short: Decay bound at $t=1$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Decay at t=c
nodes.statement_short: Decay bound at $t=c$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Equation eqn:omega-2
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}
nodes.label: eqn:omega-2

nodes.name: Decay at t=2cj^2
nodes.statement: For $t = 2cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we get \begin{align*} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{\omega(0)} &= \frac{c\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2)}{(2cj^2 - 1)(2cj^2-c)\prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} |2ci^2 - 2cj^2|} \\ &= \frac{c(m!)^2}{(4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c)\prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} (i+j)|i-j|} \\ &= \frac{c}{4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c} \cdot \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!}. \end{align*} For $j \ge 1$, the first factor is bounded by \[\frac{c}{4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c} \le \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2},\] using the fact that $c \ge 2$. We control the second factor by \begin{align*} \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!} &= \frac{m}{m+j} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m+j-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{m-j+1}{m+1} \\ &\le \left(\frac{m}{m+j} \right)^j \\ &\le \left(1 - \frac{j}{2m} \right)^j \\ &\le e^{-j^2/2m}, \end{align*} where the last inequality uses the fact that $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x$. Since \[\frac{|\omega(t)|}{\|\omega\|_1} \le \frac{|\omega(2cj^2)|}{\omega(0)} \le \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2} \cdot e^{-2cj^2/(4cm)} \le \frac{170}{\delta \cdot t^2} \cdot e^{-t \sqrt{\delta} / 10 \sqrt{T}},\] this establishes~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-decay-ref}.
nodes.statement_short: Decay bound at $t=2cj^2$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Correlation remains
nodes.statement: What remains is to perform the correlation calculation to establish~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-corr-ref}.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining: the correlation bound.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Ratio at t=1
nodes.statement: For $t = 1$, we observe \[\frac{|\omega(1)|}{\omega(0)} = \frac{c\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2)}{(c-1)\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2 - 1)} \ge \prod_{i=1}^m \frac{i^2}{i^2 - 1/(2c)} \ge 1.\]
nodes.statement_short: $|\omega(1)|\ge\omega(0)$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Tail contribution
nodes.statement: Next, we observe that the total contribution of $t > c$ to $\|\omega\|_1/\omega(0)$ is at most \begin{equation} \sum_{t > c} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{\omega(0)} \le \sum_{j=1}^{m} \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2} < \sum_{j=1}^\infty \frac{3}{4cj^4} = \frac{\pi^4}{120 c}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Tail beyond $c$ is $O(1/c)$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.statement: \sum_{t > c} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{\omega(0)} \le \sum_{j=1}^{m} \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2} < \sum_{j=1}^\infty \frac{3}{4cj^4} = \frac{\pi^4}{120 c}.
nodes.name: Equation eqn:omega-tail
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}
nodes.label: eqn:omega-tail

nodes.name: Correlation lower bound
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound the correlation.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Equation eqn:fudgethis
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}
nodes.label: eqn:fudgethis

nodes.name: Norm upper bound
nodes.statement: On the other hand, \begin{align} \|\omega\|_1 &\le \omega(0) - \omega(1) + \omega(2) + \omega(0) \cdot \frac{\pi^4}{120c} & \text{by } \eqref{eqn:omega-tail} \nonumber \\ &\le -\omega(1) + \omega(0) \left(1 + \frac{6}{c - 1} + \frac{\pi^4}{120c} \right) &\text{by } \eqref{eqn:omega-2}\nonumber \\ &\le -\omega(1) + (1 + \delta)\omega(0) & \text{since } c \ge 8/\delta. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound $\|\omega\|_1$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.statement: \|\omega\|_1 &\le \omega(0) - \omega(1) + \omega(2) + \omega(0) \cdot \frac{\pi^4}{120c} & \text{by } \eqref{eqn:omega-tail} \nonumber \\ &\le -\omega(1) + \omega(0) \left(1 + \frac{6}{c - 1} + \frac{\pi^4}{120c} \right) &\text{by } \eqref{eqn:omega-2}\nonumber \\ &\le -\omega(1) + (1 + \delta)\omega(0) & \text{since } c \ge 8/\delta.
nodes.name: Equation eqn:fudgethat
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}
nodes.label: eqn:fudgethat

nodes.name: Ratio
nodes.statement: Combining~\eqref{eqn:fudgethis} and~\eqref{eqn:fudgethat}, and using the fact that $-\omega(1) \ge \omega(0)$ shows that \[\frac{\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^k \omega(t)}{\|\omega\|_1} \ge \frac{-\omega(1) + (1-\delta) \omega(0)}{-\omega(1) + (1+\delta) \omega(0)} \ge \frac{2-\delta}{2 + \delta} \ge 1 - \delta.\] This establishes~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-corr-ref}, completing the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Ratio is at least $1-\delta$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.statement: The following construction of a dual polynomial for $\mathsf{ OR}_N$, with $N \ge T$, is an immediate consequence of Minsky-Papert symmetrization (\Cref{lem:mp}), combined with \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Symmetrize: spread $\omega(t)$ uniformly over inputs of weight $t$ (Minsky-Papert).

nodes.statement: Let $T, N \in \mathbb{N}$ with $T \le N$, and let $\delta > 1/T$. Define $\omega$ as in \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}. Define the function $\psi: \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ by $\psi(x) = \omega(|x|) / \binom{N}{ |x|}$ for $x \in H^N_{\le T}$ and $\psi(x) = 0$ otherwise. Then \begin{align} &\langle \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle \ge 1-\delta \\ & \|\psi\|_1 = 1 \\ & \text{For any polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg p < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \langle \psi, p \rangle = 0 \end{align}

nodes.statement: Let $\mathsf{ OR}_N : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ \ and \ $\mathsf{AND}_R \colon \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$. \ Let $\psi\colon \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be a function such that $\|\psi\|_1 = 1$ and $\langle \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle \ge 19/20$. Then there exists a function $\Phi \colon \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ with pure high degree $\Omega(\sqrt{R})$ and $\|\Phi\|_1 = 1$ such that \[ \langle \Phi \star \psi, \mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle > 2/3.\]

There exist $N = O(R)$, $D = \tilde{\Omega}(N^{3/4})$, and $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\sum_{x \in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}}\zeta(x) \cdot (\mathsf{AND}_{R} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N)(x) > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \text{ and } \\ &\text{ For every polynomial } p \colon (\{-1,1\}^N)^R\to \mathbb{R} \text{ of degree less than } D, \text{ we have } \langle p, \zeta \rangle = 0. \end{align}

nodes.statement: We start by fixing choices of several key parameters: \begin{itemize} \item $d= \Theta(\sqrt{R})$ is the pure high degree of the dual witness $\Phi$ for $\mathsf{AND}_R$ in \Cref{prop:and-or}, \item $T = \lfloor(R/d)^{1/2}\rfloor^2 = \Theta(\sqrt{R})$, \item $\hat{D} = c_1 \sqrt{T} \cdot d =\Theta(R^{3/4})$, where $c_1$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}, \item $\delta =1/20$ \item $\alpha = 170/\delta = 3400$, \item $\beta = c_2 \cdot \sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T} = \Theta(1/R^{1/4})$, where $c_2$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}, \item $N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R = 693 R$. \end{itemize} Let $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:or-dual} with $\delta:=1/20$. Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:and-or}, and define $\xi = \Phi \star \psi$. Then by \Cref{prop:ls}, $\xi$ satisfies the following properties: \begin{align}& \langle \xi, \mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle > 2/3, \\ & \| \xi \|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } D, \text{ we have }\langle \xi, p \rangle = 0. \end{align} Recall that $\psi$ was obtained by symmetrizing the function $\omega$ constructed in \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}. \Cref{prop:btzeroing} guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4})$, the function $\xi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle \ge \langle \xi, \mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle - \|\zeta - \xi\|_1 \ge 2/3 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*} Observing that \[D = \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4})\] shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{prop:surj-dual}.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Set parameters, combine the OR dual with the AND dual via dual block composition, then zero out the high-weight mass with the zeroing proposition.

nodes.statement: Let $k, T, N \in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \le T$. There exist constants $c_1, c_2 \in (0, 1] $ and a function $\omega : \{0, 1, \dots, T\} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{\omega(t) > 0, t \ge k} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{1}{48N} \\ & \sum_{\omega(t) < 0, t < k} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k}\right) \\ & \|\omega\|_1 := \sum_{t = 0}^{T} |\omega(t)| = 1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \notag \\ & \deg p < c_1\sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})}{t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, T. \end{align}
nodes.name: Univariate dual witness for THR
nodes.statement_short: A univariate dual for $\mathsf{THR}^k$ with tiny false-positive mass, bounded false-negative mass, pure high degree $\Omega(\sqrt{TN^{-1/k}/k})$ and exponential tail decay.
conclusions: There exist constants $c_1, c_2 \in (0, 1] $ and a function $\omega : \{0, 1, \dots, T\} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{\omega(t) > 0, t \ge k} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{1}{48N} \\ & \sum_{\omega(t) < 0, t < k} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k}\right) \\ & \|\omega\|_1 := \sum_{t = 0}^{T} |\omega(t)| = 1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \notag \\ & \deg p < c_1\sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})}{t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, T. \end{align}
