nodes.statement: If $k = 1$, then the function defined by $\omega(0) = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\omega(1) = -\frac{1}{2}$ satisfies the conditions of the proposition for $c_1 = c_2 = 1$. In what follows, we treat the complementary case where $k \ge 2$. Let $E_+ := \{t \colon \omega(t) > 0, t \ge k\}$, and $E_{-} := \{t\colon \omega(t) < 0, t < k\}$. By normalizing, it suffices to construct a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{1}{48 N} \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \nonumber \\ &\deg p < c_1\sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \sum_{t=0}^k \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})\|\omega\|_1}{t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, T. \end{align} Let $c = 2k\lceil N^{1/k}\rceil$, and let $m = \lfloor \sqrt{T/c} \rfloor$. Define the set \[S = \{1, 2, \dots, k\} \cup \{ci^2 : 0 \le i \le m\}.\] Note that $|S| = \Omega(k^{-1/2}T^{1/2}N^{-1/(2k)})$. Define the polynomial \[\omega(t) = \frac{(-1)^{t+(T-m)+1}}{T!} \binom{T}{t} \prod_{r \in [T]_0 \setminus S} (t - r).\] The signs are chosen so that $\omega(k) < 0$. It is immediate from \Cref{fact:combinatorial} that $\omega$ satisfies~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-phd-ref} for $c_1 = 1/\sqrt{2}$. We now show that~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} holds. For $t = 1, \dots, k$, we have \[\frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})}{t^2} \ge \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 \sqrt{k})}{k^2} \ge 1\] as long as $c_2 \le 1/2$ and $k \ge 2$. Since $|\omega(t)| \le \|\omega\|_1$, the bound holds for $t = 1, \dots, k$. For $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we expand out the binomial coefficient in the definition of $\omega$ to obtain \[|\omega(t)| = \begin{cases} \prod\limits_{r \in S\setminus \{t\}} \frac{1}{|t - r|} & \text{ for } t \in S, \\ 0 & \text{ otherwise.} \end{cases}\] For $t \in \{0, 1, \dots, k\}$, we observe that \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} = \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - k)}{t! \cdot (k - t)! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - t)} \le \binom{k}{t}. \end{equation} Meanwhile, for $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we get \begin{align*} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} &= \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (ci^2 - k)}{\prod_{i = 1}^k(cj^2 - i) \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} |ci^2 - cj^2|} \\ &\le \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m ci^2}{(cj^2 - k)^{k} \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} c(i+j)|i-j|} \\ &= \frac{k!}{j(cj^2 - k)^{k}} \cdot \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!}. \end{align*} The first factor is bounded above by \[\frac{k!}{(c - k)^k j^{2k+1}}.\] As long as $c \ge 2k$ and $k \ge 2$, this expression is at most \[\frac{k^k}{(c/2)^kj^4} = \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4}.\] We control the second factor by \begin{align*} \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!} &= \frac{m}{m+j} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m+j-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{m-j+1}{m+1} \\ &\le \left(\frac{m}{m+j} \right)^j \\ &\le \left(1 - \frac{j}{2m} \right)^j \\ &\le e^{-j^2/2m}, \end{align*} where the last inequality uses the fact that $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x$. Hence, \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m}. \end{equation} This immediately yields \[\frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{\|\omega\|_1} \le \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{(cj^2)^2} \cdot e^{-cj^2/(2cm)},\] which establishes~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} for all $t = cj^2 > k$. Moreover, by \eqref{eqn:tail-bound} \begin{equation} \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j = 1}^m \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k} \cdot |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{1}{j^4} \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N}. \end{equation} Hence, since $\omega(k) < 0$, \[\sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N} \le \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{48N},\] which gives~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-pos-corr-ref}. Finally, to establish~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-neg-corr-ref}, we combine ~\eqref{eqn:head-bound} and~\eqref{eqn:tail-sum} to obtain \begin{equation} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{|\omega(k)|} \le \sum_{t = 0}^k \binom{k}{t} + \frac{1}{48 N} < 2^k + 1 < \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4^k. \end{equation} We calculate \begin{align*} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{2} - \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| &= \sum_{t : \omega(t) < 0} (-\omega(t)) - \sum_{t \in E_-} (-\omega(t)) & \text{since $\langle \omega, \mathbf{1} \rangle = 0$}\\ &= \sum_{t \colon \omega(t) < 0, t \geq k} (-\omega(t)) \\ &\ge -\omega(k). \end{align*} Rearranging and applying the bound~\eqref{eqn:mass-on-k}, \[\sum_{t \in E_{-}} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\omega(k)}{\|\omega\|_1}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2 \cdot 4^{-k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1.\]
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Explicit construction of $\omega$ supported on $\{1,\dots,k\}\cup\{ci^2\}$; bound its values relative to $|\omega(k)|$ to get decay and the one-sided error bounds.

nodes.name: Case k=1
nodes.statement: If $k = 1$, then the function defined by $\omega(0) = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\omega(1) = -\frac{1}{2}$ satisfies the conditions of the proposition for $c_1 = c_2 = 1$. In what follows, we treat the complementary case where $k \ge 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial witness for $k=1$; treat $k\ge2$.

nodes.name: Unnormalised goal
nodes.statement: Let $E_+ := \{t \colon \omega(t) > 0, t \ge k\}$, and $E_{-} := \{t\colon \omega(t) < 0, t < k\}$. By normalizing, it suffices to construct a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{1}{48 N} \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \nonumber \\ &\deg p < c_1\sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \sum_{t=0}^k \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})\|\omega\|_1}{t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, T. \end{align}

nodes.name: Construct omega
nodes.statement: Let $c = 2k\lceil N^{1/k}\rceil$, and let $m = \lfloor \sqrt{T/c} \rfloor$. Define the set \[S = \{1, 2, \dots, k\} \cup \{ci^2 : 0 \le i \le m\}.\] Note that $|S| = \Omega(k^{-1/2}T^{1/2}N^{-1/(2k)})$. Define the polynomial \[\omega(t) = \frac{(-1)^{t+(T-m)+1}}{T!} \binom{T}{t} \prod_{r \in [T]_0 \setminus S} (t - r).\]
nodes.statement_short: Define $c$, $m$, $S$ and $\omega$.

nodes.name: Pure high degree
nodes.statement: The signs are chosen so that $\omega(k) < 0$. It is immediate from \Cref{fact:combinatorial} that $\omega$ satisfies~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-phd-ref} for $c_1 = 1/\sqrt{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Sign convention and pure high degree via the binomial identity.

nodes.name: Decay for small t
nodes.statement: We now show that~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} holds. For $t = 1, \dots, k$, we have \[\frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})}{t^2} \ge \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 \sqrt{k})}{k^2} \ge 1\] as long as $c_2 \le 1/2$ and $k \ge 2$. Since $|\omega(t)| \le \|\omega\|_1$, the bound holds for $t = 1, \dots, k$.
nodes.statement_short: Decay bound for $t\le k$.

nodes.name: Bound is at least 1
nodes.statement: For $t = 1, \dots, k$, we have \[\frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})}{t^2} \ge \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 \sqrt{k})}{k^2} \ge 1\] as long as $c_2 \le 1/2$ and $k \ge 2$.
nodes.statement_short: The decay bound exceeds 1 for $t\le k$.

nodes.name: Holds trivially
nodes.statement: Since $|\omega(t)| \le \|\omega\|_1$, the bound holds for $t = 1, \dots, k$.
nodes.statement_short: So it holds for $t\le k$.

nodes.name: Formula for |omega|
nodes.statement: For $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we expand out the binomial coefficient in the definition of $\omega$ to obtain \[|\omega(t)| = \begin{cases} \prod\limits_{r \in S\setminus \{t\}} \frac{1}{|t - r|} & \text{ for } t \in S, \\ 0 & \text{ otherwise.} \end{cases}\]
nodes.statement_short: Closed form for $|\omega(t)|$.

nodes.name: Head bound
nodes.statement: For $t \in \{0, 1, \dots, k\}$, we observe that \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} = \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - k)}{t! \cdot (k - t)! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - t)} \le \binom{k}{t}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Head values are at most $\binom{k}{t}|\omega(k)|$.

nodes.statement: \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} = \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - k)}{t! \cdot (k - t)! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - t)} \le \binom{k}{t}.
nodes.name: Equation eqn:head-bound
nodes.label: eqn:head-bound

nodes.name: First factor
nodes.statement: Meanwhile, for $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we get \begin{align*} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} &= \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (ci^2 - k)}{\prod_{i = 1}^k(cj^2 - i) \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} |ci^2 - cj^2|} \\ &\le \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m ci^2}{(cj^2 - k)^{k} \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} c(i+j)|i-j|} \\ &= \frac{k!}{j(cj^2 - k)^{k}} \cdot \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!}. \end{align*} The first factor is bounded above by \[\frac{k!}{(c - k)^k j^{2k+1}}.\] As long as $c \ge 2k$ and $k \ge 2$, this expression is at most \[\frac{k^k}{(c/2)^kj^4} = \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Bound the first factor of the tail ratio.

nodes.name: Second factor
nodes.statement: We control the second factor by \begin{align*} \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!} &= \frac{m}{m+j} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m+j-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{m-j+1}{m+1} \\ &\le \left(\frac{m}{m+j} \right)^j \\ &\le \left(1 - \frac{j}{2m} \right)^j \\ &\le e^{-j^2/2m}, \end{align*} where the last inequality uses the fact that $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x$. Hence, \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the second factor; tail bound.

nodes.statement: \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m}.
nodes.name: Equation eqn:tail-bound
nodes.label: eqn:tail-bound

nodes.name: Decay for large t
nodes.statement: This immediately yields \[\frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{\|\omega\|_1} \le \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{(cj^2)^2} \cdot e^{-cj^2/(2cm)},\] which establishes~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} for all $t = cj^2 > k$.
nodes.statement_short: Decay bound for $t=cj^2>k$.

nodes.name: False-positive mass
nodes.statement: Moreover, by \eqref{eqn:tail-bound} \begin{equation} \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j = 1}^m \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k} \cdot |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{1}{j^4} \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N}. \end{equation} Hence, since $\omega(k) < 0$, \[\sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N} \le \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{48N},\] which gives~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-pos-corr-ref}.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the tail to bound false positives.

nodes.statement: \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j = 1}^m \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k} \cdot |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{1}{j^4} \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N}.
nodes.name: Equation eqn:tail-sum
nodes.label: eqn:tail-sum

nodes.name: False-negative mass
nodes.statement: Finally, to establish~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-neg-corr-ref}, we combine ~\eqref{eqn:head-bound} and~\eqref{eqn:tail-sum} to obtain \begin{equation} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{|\omega(k)|} \le \sum_{t = 0}^k \binom{k}{t} + \frac{1}{48 N} < 2^k + 1 < \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4^k. \end{equation} We calculate \begin{align*} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{2} - \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| &= \sum_{t : \omega(t) < 0} (-\omega(t)) - \sum_{t \in E_-} (-\omega(t)) & \text{since $\langle \omega, \mathbf{1} \rangle = 0$}\\ &= \sum_{t \colon \omega(t) < 0, t \geq k} (-\omega(t)) \\ &\ge -\omega(k). \end{align*} Rearranging and applying the bound~\eqref{eqn:mass-on-k}, \[\sum_{t \in E_{-}} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\omega(k)}{\|\omega\|_1}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2 \cdot 4^{-k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1.\]
nodes.statement_short: Bound false-negative mass via mass on $k$.

nodes.statement: \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{|\omega(k)|} \le \sum_{t = 0}^k \binom{k}{t} + \frac{1}{48 N} < 2^k + 1 < \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4^k.
nodes.name: Equation eqn:mass-on-k
nodes.label: eqn:mass-on-k

nodes.statement: Applying Minsky-Papert symmetrization (\Cref{lem:mp}) to ensure that the resulting function has the appropriate pure high degree, \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual} yields a dual polynomial for $\mathsf{THR}^k_N$.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Symmetrize the univariate THR dual witness (Minsky-Papert).

nodes.statement: Let $k, T, N\in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \le T \le N$. Define $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\psi(x) = \omega(|x|) / \binom{N}{ |x|}$ for $x \in H_{\le T}^N$ and $\psi(x) = 0$ otherwise, where $\omega$ is as constructed in \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}. Then \begin{align} &\sum_{x \in E_+(\psi, \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |\psi(x)| \le \frac{1}{48 N} \\ &\sum_{x \in E_-(\psi, \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |\psi(x)| \le \frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k} \\ &\|\psi\|_1 = 1 \\ &\text{For any polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg p < c_1 \sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \langle \psi, p \rangle = 0 \\ &\sum_{|x| = t} |\psi(x)| \le (2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})/t^2 \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, N. \end{align}
nodes.name: Dual polynomial for THR^k_N

conclusions: \begin{align} &\sum_{x \in E_+(\psi, \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |\psi(x)| \le \frac{1}{48 N} \\ &\sum_{x \in E_-(\psi, \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |\psi(x)| \le \frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k} \\ &\|\psi\|_1 = 1 \\ &\text{For any polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg p < c_1 \sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \langle \psi, p \rangle = 0 \\ &\sum_{|x| = t} |\psi(x)| \le (2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})/t^2 \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, N. \end{align}
nodes.label: prop:thr-dual

nodes.statement: &\text{For any polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg p < c_1 \sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \langle \psi, p \rangle = 0 \\ &\sum_{|x| = t} |\psi(x)| \le (2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})/t^2 \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, N.

nodes.statement: Let $f : \{-1,1\}^m \to \{-1,1\}$ and $\psi : \{-1,1\}^m \to \mathbb{R}$ be functions such that \begin{align} &\sum_{x \in E_+(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le \delta^+ \\ & \sum_{x \in E_-(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le \delta^- \\ & \|\psi\|_1 = 1. \end{align} For every $M \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists a function $\varphi : \{-1,1\}^M \to \{-1,1\}$ with $\|\varphi\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $1$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{x \in E_+(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le M \cdot \delta^+ \\ & \sum_{x \in E_-(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le \frac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^M. \end{align}
nodes.name: Error amplification
nodes.statement_short: Composing with a dual for $\mathsf{OR}_M$ multiplies false-positive error by at most $M$ and shrinks false-negative error to $(2\delta^-)^M/2$.
assumptions: $f : \{-1,1\}^m \to \{-1,1\}$ and $\psi : \{-1,1\}^m \to \mathbb{R}$ be functions such that \begin{align} &\sum_{x \in E_+(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le \delta^+ \\ & \sum_{x \in E_-(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le \delta^- \\ & \|\psi\|_1 = 1. \end{align}
conclusions: there exists a function $\varphi : \{-1,1\}^M \to \{-1,1\}$ with $\|\varphi\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $1$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{x \in E_+(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le M \cdot \delta^+ \\ & \sum_{x \in E_-(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le \frac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^M. \end{align}
nodes.label: prop:error-amp

nodes.label: eqn:error-amp-pos

nodes.statement:
Let $\varphi: \{-1, 1\}^M ightarrow \{-1, 1\}$ be defined such that $\varphi(\mathbf{1})=1/2$, $\varphi(-\mathbf{1})=-1/2$, and $\varphi(x)=0$ for all other $x$. Notice that  egin{equation} \sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in \{-1, 1\}^M} \varphi(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) = 0 \end{equation} so $\Psi$ has pure high degree $1$, and that $\|\Psi\|_1 = 1$. We now prove that (\Cref{eqn:error-amp-pos}) holds. Let $\lambda$ be the distribution on $\{-1, 1\}^{m}$ given by $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$, and let $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ be the product distribution on $(\{-1, 1\}^m)^M$ given by $\lambda^{\otimes M}(x_1, \dots, x_M) = \prod_{i=1}^M |\psi(x_i)|$. Since $\psi$ is orthogonal to the constant polynomial, it has expected value 0, and hence the string $(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots)$ is distributed uniformly in $\{-1, 1\}^{M}$ when one samples $(x_1, \dots, x_{M})$ according to $\lambda^{\otimes M}$. This allows us to write  egin{align} &\hspace{-2em}\sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in E^+(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M)| 
onumber \ &\hspace{-2em}= 2^{M} \mathbf{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\varphi( \dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) \cdot \mathbb{I} (\varphi( \dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) > 0 \land \mathsf{ OR}_M\left( \dots, f(x_i), \dotsight) = -1)] 
onumber\ &\hspace{-2em}= \sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) = -1 | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z]. \end{align} Observe that for any bit $b$, \[\Pr_{x \sim \lambda} [f(x) 
e \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x)) | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x)) = b] = 2\sum_{x \in A_b} |\psi(x)|,\] where for brevity, we have written $A_{+1} = E_+(\psi, f)$ and $A_{-1} = E_-(\psi, f)$. Therefore, as noted in \cite{sherstovhalfspaces1}, for any given $z \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$, the following two random variables are identically distributed:  egin{itemize} \item The string $(\dots, f(x_i), \dots)$, when one chooses $(\dots, x_i, \dots)$ from $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ conditioned on 
ewline $(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z$ \item The string $(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots)$, where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. \end{itemize} Thus, Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle} equals  egin{equation}\sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots) = -1], \end{equation} where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. The only term in this sum corresponds to $z=\mathbf{1}$, which we now argue is at most $M \delta^+$. By \eqref{eqn:error-base-pos}, each $y_i = -1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^+(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^+$. Hence, for $z = \mathbf{1}$, we have \[\Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1] \le 2 M \delta^+\] by a union bound. Thus Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle2} is at most $M \delta^+$, proving \eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}. It now remains to prove the bound~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-neg}. By an identical argument as above, we have  egin{equation}\sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in E^-(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M)| = \sum_{z : \varphi(z) < 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots) = 1]. \end{equation} The only term in the sum corresponds to $z=-\mathbf{1}$, which we argue takes value $ rac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^{M}$. Here, each $y_i=-1$ independently with probability $\sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^-(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^-$, and $\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, -y_i, \dots)=1$ only if $y_i = -1$ for every $i$. Hence, we conclude that \[\Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_{M}\left(\dots, -y_i, \dotsight) = 1] \le (2\delta^-)^M. \] It follows that Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-end} is at most $ rac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^M$, establishing~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}. This completes the proof.

We now prove that (\Cref{eqn:error-amp-pos}) holds. Let $\lambda$ be the distribution on $\{-1, 1\}^{m}$ given by $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$, and let $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ be the product distribution on $(\{-1, 1\}^m)^M$ given by $\lambda^{\otimes M}(x_1, \dots, x_M) = \prod_{i=1}^M |\psi(x_i)|$. Since $\psi$ is orthogonal to the constant polynomial, it has expected value 0, and hence the string $(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots)$ is distributed uniformly in $\{-1, 1\}^{M}$ when one samples $(x_1, \dots, x_{M})$ according to $\lambda^{\otimes M}$. onumber\ &\hspace{-2em}= \sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) = -1 | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z]. \end{align} Observe that for any bit $b$, \[\Pr_{x \sim \lambda} [f(x) 
e \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x)) | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x)) = b] = 2\sum_{x \in A_b} |\psi(x)|,\] where for brevity, we have written $A_{+1} = E_+(\psi, f)$ and $A_{-1} = E_-(\psi, f)$. Therefore, as noted in \cite{sherstovhalfspaces1}, for any given $z \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$, the following two random variables are identically distributed:  egin{itemize} \item The string $(\dots, f(x_i), \dots)$, when one chooses $(\dots, x_i, \dots)$ from $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ conditioned on 
ewline $(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z$ \item The string $(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots)$, where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. \end{itemize} Thus, Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle} equals  egin{equation}\sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots) = -1], \end{equation} where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. The only term in this sum corresponds to $z=\mathbf{1}$, which we now argue is at most $M \delta^+$. By \eqref{eqn:error-base-pos}, each $y_i = -1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^+(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^+$. Hence, for $z = \mathbf{1}$, we have \[\Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1] \le 2 M \delta^+\] by a union bound. Thus Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle2} is at most $M \delta^+$, proving \eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}.

nodes.name: Equation eqn:error-amp-middle2

nodes.name: All bits flipped
nodes.statement: The only term in the sum corresponds to $z=-\mathbf{1}$, which we argue takes value $\frac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^{M}$. Here, each $y_i=-1$ independently with probability $\sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^-(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^-$, and $\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, -y_i, \dots)=1$ only if $y_i = -1$ for every $i$. Hence, we conclude that \[\Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_{M}\left(\dots, -y_i, \dots\right) = 1] \le (2\delta^-)^M. \]
nodes.statement_short: All $M$ bits must flip: $(2\delta^-)^M$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: It follows that Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-end} is at most $\frac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^M$, establishing~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}. This completes the proof.

Let $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function with $\|\psi\|_1 = 1$ and \begin{align*} &\sum_{x \in E_+(\psi, \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |\psi(x)| \le \frac{1}{48 N} \\ &\sum_{x \in E_-(\psi, \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |\psi(x)| \le \frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k}. \end{align*} Then there exists a function $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\Phi\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(2^{-k} \sqrt{R})$ such that \[ \langle \Phi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N \rangle \ge 2/3. \]

nodes.statement: Using the construction of \Cref{prop:error-amp} with $m = N$, $M = 4^k$, and $f = \mathsf{THR}_N^k$, we first obtain a function $\varphi : \{-1,1\}^{4^k} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\varphi\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $1$ such that \begin{align*} &\sum_{x \in E_+(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le \frac{4^k}{48 N} \\ &\sum_{x \in E_-(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 4 \cdot 4^{-k} \right)^{4^k} \le \frac{e^{-4}}{2}. \end{align*} Now by the construction of \Cref{prop:degree-amp} with $m = 4^k \cdot N$, $M = R/4^{k}$ and $f = \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k$, there exists a function $\rho : \{-1,1\}^{R / 4^k} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\rho\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(2^{-k}\sqrt{R})$ such that \[ \langle \rho \star (\varphi \star \psi), \mathsf{ OR}_{R/4^k} \circ (\mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N) \rangle \ge \frac{9}{10} - \frac{4R}{48 N} - 2e^{-4} \ge \frac{2}{3}.\] Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \mathbb{R}$ be the dual block composition $\rho \star \varphi$. Since the dual block composition preserves $\ell_1$-norms (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-norm}) and multiplies pure high degrees (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-phd}), the function $\Phi$ itself has $\ell_1$-norm $1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(2^{-k} \sqrt{R})$. The claim now follows from the associativity of dual block composition (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-assoc}) and the fact that $\mathsf{ OR}_R = \mathsf{ OR}_{R/4^k} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k}$.

Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:dist-prelim}, and define $\xi = \Phi \star \psi$. Then by \Cref{prop:ls}, $\xi$ satisfies the following properties: \begin{align}& \langle \xi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle > 2/3, \\ & \| \xi \|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \hat{D}, \text{ we have }\langle \xi, p \rangle = 0. \end{align} Recall that $\psi$ was obtained by symmetrizing the function $\omega$ constructed in \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}. \Cref{prop:btzeroing} guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/4} \cdot R^{3/4 - 1/(2k)})$, the function $\xi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle \ge \langle \xi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle - \|\zeta - \xi\|_1 \ge 2/3 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*} Observing that \[D = \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/ 4} \cdot R^{3/4-1/(2k)})\] shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{prop:dist-dual}.

Then by \Cref{prop:ls}, $\xi$ satisfies the following properties: \begin{align}& \langle \xi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle > 2/3, \\ & \| \xi \|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \hat{D}, \text{ we have }\langle \xi, p \rangle = 0. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Compose the OR and THR duals.

nodes.statement: & \langle \xi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle > 2/3, \\ & \| \xi \|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \hat{D}, \text{ we have }\langle \xi, p \rangle = 0.

Recall symmetrization
nodes.statement: Recall that $\psi$ was obtained by symmetrizing the function $\omega$ constructed in \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}.
nodes.statement_short: Recall $\psi$ comes from $\omega$.

nodes.name: Zero out
nodes.statement: \Cref{prop:btzeroing} guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/4} \cdot R^{3/4 - 1/(2k)})$, the function $\xi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle \ge \langle \xi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle - \|\zeta - \xi\|_1 \ge 2/3 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Zero out high-weight mass.

nodes.name: Degree
nodes.statement: Observing that \[D = \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/ 4} \cdot R^{3/4-1/(2k)})\] shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{prop:dist-dual}.
nodes.statement_short: Pure high degree $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4-1/(2k)})$.

nodes.statement: \Cref{thm:dist-promise} now follows by combining \Cref{prop:dist-dual} with the dual characterization of unbounded approximate degree \Cref{prop:ub-duality}.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Combine the final OR-THR dual witness with the dual characterization of unbounded approximate degree.

nodes.statement: The approximate degree lower bound in \Cref{thm:dist} is then a consequence of \Cref{prop:dumdist-reduction} and \Cref{cor:dist-reduction}. The quantum query lower bound follows via the standard fact that the $\varepsilon$-error quantum query complexity of $f$ is lower bounded by $1/2 \cdot \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{2\varepsilon}(f)$ \cite{beals}.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Chain through the dDIST reductions; the quantum bound follows from the polynomial method.

nodes.statement: Given an input $s=(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, and $i \in [R]$, let $f_i = |\{j \colon s_j=i\}|$. The \emph{image size} of $s$ is the number of $i \in [R]$ such that $f_i > 0$. For $0 < \gamma < 1$, define: $$\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{ if the image size is } R\\ 1 & \text{ if the image size is at most } \gamma \cdot R\\ \text{undefined} & \text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$
nodes.name: Image Size Testing function
nodes.statement_short: Partial function: $-1$ if all $R$ range items appear, $+1$ if at most $\gamma R$ appear, undefined otherwise.

nodes.statement: For some constant $c > 0$, and any constant $\gamma \in (0, 1)$, $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right) \ge \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$, where $N = c \cdot \gamma^{-1/2} \cdot R$. The same lower bound applies to the quantum query complexity of $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$.
nodes.name: Approximate degree lower bound for Image Size Testing
assumptions: For some constant $c > 0$, and any constant $\gamma \in (0, 1)$
conclusions: $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right) \ge \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$
The same lower bound applies to the quantum query complexity of $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$

nodes.statement: It is possible to refine our analysis to show that even the \emph{unbounded} approximate degree of $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ is $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$, and that this holds even if the error parameter is $1-2^{-n^{\Omega(1)}}$. However, for brevity we do not explicitly establish this stronger result. We direct the interested reader to subsequent work \cite{btlargeerror}, which shows that the threshold degree of $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}$ is $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$ for $R \leq N/2$. The proof of that result can be extended with little difficulty to show that the threshold degree of $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ is $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$.
nodes.name: Refinement to unbounded approximate degree and large error

nodes.statement: Let $Y \subset \{-1,1\}^R$ and $f \colon Y \to \{-1,1\}$, and let $g \colon \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be a symmetric (total) function. Let $G = \{x_1, \dots, x_R \colon (g(x_1), \dots, g(x_R)) \in Y\}.$ Let $F^{\le N}$ be defined as above. Observe that $F^{\le N}$ is defined at all inputs in $H_{\leq N}^{N \cdot R} \cap G$. The double-promise $\varepsilon$-approximate degree of $F^{\le N}$, denoted $\widetilde{\operatorname{dpdeg}}(F^{\le N})$ is the least degree of a real polynomial $p$ such that: \begin{align} & |p(x) - F^{\le N}(x)| \leq \varepsilon \text{ for all } x \in H_{\leq N}^{N \cdot R} \cap G.\\ & |p(x)| \leq 1+\varepsilon \text{ for all } x \in H_{\leq N}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G. \end{align}
nodes.name: Double-promise approximate degree
nodes.statement_short: Least degree of a polynomial approximating $F^{\le N}$ on weight-$\le N$ inputs in $G$ and bounded on other weight-$\le N$ inputs.

nodes.statement: Define $\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \colon H_{\leq (\gamma \cdot R)}^R \cup \{\mathbf{-1}\} \to \{-1,1\}$ via: $$\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma}(x) = \begin{cases} -1 & \text { if } x_i=-1 \text{ for all } i \\ 1 & \text{ if } x\in H_{\leq (\gamma \cdot R)}^R\\ \text{undefined} & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$
nodes.name: Gap AND function
also_stated_at: Here, $\mathsf{GapAND}_R$ is the promise function that outputs $-1$ if all of its inputs equal $-1$, outputs $+1$ if fewer than $\gamma \cdot R$ of its inputs are $-1$, and is undefined otherwise.

nodes.statement: In the case where $f = \mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma}$ and $g = \mathsf{ OR}_N$, the function $F^{\operatorname{prop}}(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ is precisely the $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^\gamma$ function.

nodes.statement: Let $N, R \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $Y$ be the domain of $\mathsf{GapAND}_R^{\gamma}$, and let $G=\{(x_1, \dots, x_R) \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \colon (\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_1), \dots, \mathsf{ OR}_N(x_R)) \in Y\}.$ Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^\gamma) \ge \widetilde{\operatorname{dpdeg}}_\varepsilon(F^{\le N})\] where $F^{\le N} : G \cap H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N} \to \{-1,1\}$ is the partial function obtained by restricting $\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ to $H^{N\cdot R}_{\le N}$.

nodes.statement: We construct a dual polynomial to witness the lower bound in \Cref{sethm}. Define the parameters \begin{itemize} \item $\delta = \gamma/4$, \item $\alpha = 170/\delta$, \item $T=N=\lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R \leq 310 \cdot \gamma^{-1/2} \cdot R$, \item $\beta = c_2 \cdot \sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T}$, where $c_2$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}. \end{itemize} Let $\psi$ be the dual witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_N$ from \Cref{prop:or-dual} with $T=N$. Define $\Phi \colon \{-1,1\}^R \to \mathbb{R}$ as follows: $$\Phi(x) = \begin{cases} -1/2 & \text{ if } x=(-1, -1, \dots, -1)\\ 1/2 & \text{ if } x = (1, 1, \dots, 1)\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$ The dual block composition $\Phi \star \psi$ is the same dual witness for $\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ which Bun and Thaler \cite{bt14} used to show that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N) = \Omega(N^{1/2})$ for $\varepsilon = 1-2^{-R}$. This dual witness was also used in subsequent works \cite{sherstov14, bchtv}. Curiously, we are interested in this dual witness for a completely different reason than these prior works. These prior works were interested in $\Phi \star \psi$ because its correlation with the target function $\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ is exponentially closer to 1 than is the correlation of $\psi$ with $\mathsf{ OR}_N$. For our purposes, it will not be essential to exploit such a strong correlation guarantee---rather, we are interested in $\Phi \star \psi$ because most its ``$\ell_1$-mass'' lies on inputs either with full image or tiny image (i.e., most of its mass lies in the domain of $\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$). As in \Cref{cor:se-reduction}, let $G$ denote the set of all inputs on which $\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ is defined, i.e., $$G=\{x_1, \dots, x_R \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \colon (\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_1), \dots, \mathsf{ OR}_N(x_R)) \in H_{\leq \gamma \cdot R}^R \cup \{\mathbf{-1}\}\}.$$ The analysis in these prior works \cite{bt14,bchtv} implies that $\Phi \star \psi$ satisfies the following three properties. \begin{align} &\|\Phi \star \psi \|_1=1, \\ &\sum_{x \in G} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \geq 9/10, \\ &\text{For any polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^{N\cdot R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg p < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \langle \Phi \star \psi, p \rangle = 0, \end{align} where $c_1$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-dual}. Indeed, Properties~\eqref{ughnorm} and~\eqref{ughphd} are immediate from \Cref{prop:ls} on the properties of dual block composition. For completeness, we prove that Property~\eqref{ughcor} holds in \Cref{sec:gap-and-corr} below, making use of the fact that $\delta = \gamma/4$ and taking $R$ to be sufficiently large. \Cref{prop:btzeroing} (with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ set as above) guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$, the function $\Phi \star \psi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle \ge \langle \Phi \star \psi, \mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle - \|\zeta - \Phi \star \psi\|_1 \ge 9/10 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } D:=\min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*} Observing that \[D = \min\{c_1\sqrt{\delta T}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})\] shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{sethm} via \Cref{prop:dualitydiedie}.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Use Bun-Thaler's dual witness $\Phi\star\psi$ for $\mathsf{AND}_R\circ\mathsf{OR}_N$, which puts most mass in the domain of GapAND$\circ$OR, then zero out high-weight mass.

nodes.statement: Let $\delta > 0$, $\gamma > 2\delta$, and let $$G=\{x_1, \dots, x_R \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \colon (\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_1), \dots, \mathsf{ OR}_N(x_R)) \in H_{\leq \gamma \cdot R}^R \cup \{\mathbf{-1}\}\}.$$ Define $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ by $\Phi(-\mathbf{1}) = -1/2$, $\Phi(\mathbf{1}) = 1/2$ and $\Phi(z) = 0$ otherwise. Let $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be any dual witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_N$ such that $\|\psi\|_1 = 1$, $\langle \psi, \mathbf{1}\rangle = 0$, and $\langle \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle \ge 1 - \delta$. Then \[\sum_{x \in G} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \geq 1-\delta^R -\exp(-(\gamma - \delta) R/3).\]

assumptions: $$G=\{x_1, \dots, x_R \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \colon (\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_1), \dots, \mathsf{ OR}_N(x_R)) \in H_{\leq \gamma \cdot R}^R \cup \{\mathbf{-1}\}\}.$$
$\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be any dual witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_N$ such that $\|\psi\|_1 = 1$, $\langle \psi, \mathbf{1}\rangle = 0$, and $\langle \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle \ge 1 - \delta$
conclusions: \[\sum_{x \in G} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \geq 1-\delta^R -\exp(-(\gamma - \delta) R/3).\]
nodes.label: lem:ughcor

nodes.statement: Let $f : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ and let $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}$. We say that $\psi$ has one-sided error with respect to $f$ if for all $x \in \{-1,1\}^N$, \begin{equation} f(x) = 1 \implies \psi(x) > 0. \end{equation}
nodes.name: One-sided error

nodes.statement: f(x) = 1 \implies \psi(x) > 0.
nodes.name: Equation (unlabelled)

nodes.statement: Let $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function with pure high degree at least $1$ such that $\langle \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle > 0$. Then $\psi$ has one-sided error with respect to $\mathsf{ OR}_N$.
nodes.name: One-sided error of OR dual witnesses (Gavinsky-Sherstov)
assumptions: $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function with pure high degree at least $1$ such that $\langle \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle > 0$
conclusions: $\psi$ has one-sided error with respect to $\mathsf{ OR}_N$
nodes.label: lem:gs

nodes.statement: In particular, if $\psi$ is such a dual witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_N$, then we have \begin{equation} \sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x)| \le \frac{1}{2}(1 - \langle \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle), \qquad \sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 0, \end{equation} where the sets $A_{+1}$ and $A_{-1}$ are, respectively, the sets of false positive and false negative errors given by \begin{align*} &A_{+1} = E_+(\psi, \mathsf{ OR}_N) = \{x \in \{-1,1\}^N : \psi(x) > 0, \mathsf{ OR}_N(x) = -1\}, \\ &A_{-1} = E_-(\psi, \mathsf{ OR}_N) = \{x \in \{-1,1\}^N : \psi(x) < 0, \mathsf{ OR}_N(x) = +1\}. \end{align*}
nodes.name: Error masses of a dual witness for OR
assumptions: if $\psi$ is such a dual witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_N$
conclusions: \begin{equation} \sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x)| \le \frac{1}{2}(1 - \langle \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle), \qquad \sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 0, \end{equation}

nodes.statement: \sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x)| \le \frac{1}{2}(1 - \langle \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle), \qquad \sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 0,
nodes.name: Error mass of OR dual witnesses
nodes.label: eqn:mybullshitequation

nodes.statement:
We begin by observing that the quantity of interest can be written as  egin{align} &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_Night)(x) - 
onumber \ &\qquad\qquad \left( \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_Night)(x) + \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| ight) 
onumber \ \ge &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_Night)(x) - 2 \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|. \end{align} We estimate each term of Expression~\eqref{eqn:buttz} separately, beginning with the first term. Just as in the proofs of \Cref{prop:error-amp} and \Cref{prop:degree-amp}, we have  egin{align*} \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} (\Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot (\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N)(x) &= \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} \Phi(z) \cdot \mathbb{E}_y[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)] \end{align*} where $y \in \{-1,1\}^R$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes the value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. For $z = -\mathbf{1}$, we have by~\eqref{eqn:mybullshitequation} that $2 \sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 0$, so the contribution of the corresponding term to the sum is $1/2$. For $z = \mathbf{1}$, we use the fact that $2 \sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x)| \le \delta$ to compute  egin{align*}  rac{1}{2} \cdot \mathbb{E}_{y}[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i, \dots)] &=  rac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 2\Pr_y[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1 ] ight) \ &\ge  rac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 2\delta^Right). \end{align*} Hence, the first summand of~\eqref{eqn:buttz} is at least $1-\delta^R$. We now estimate the second summand, $2 \sum_{x 
otin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|$. As in the proofs of \Cref{prop:error-amp} and \Cref{prop:degree-amp}, we let $\lambda$ denote the distribution with probability mass function $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$. Then  egin{align*}\hspace{-2.2em} 2\sum_{x 
otin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| &= 2^{R+1} \mathbb{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes R}} [|\Phi(\dots, \operatorname{sgn} \psi(x_i), \dots)| \cdot \mathbb{I}(x 
otin G)] \ &= 2\sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} |\Phi(z)| \cdot \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z] \ &= \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{-1}] + \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{1}]. \end{align*} We analyze each term of this sum separately. For the first term, observe that by one-sided error of $\psi$, it follows that if $x = (x_1, \dots, x_R)$ is any input $\operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = -1$ for all $i$ then $\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1$ for all $i$. Thus we are guaranteed that $x \in G$, so the contribution of the first summand is zero. To analyze the second summand, let us denote by $r_i \in \{0, 1\}$ the indicator random variable for the event $\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1$ when $x_i$ is drawn from the conditional distribution $(\lambda | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = 1)$. Then  egin{align*} \Pr[r_i = 1] &= \Pr_{x_i \sim \lambda}[\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1 | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = 1] \ &= 2\sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x_i)| \ &\le \delta \end{align*} by~\eqref{eqn:mybullshitequation}. Hence,  egin{align*} \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{1}] &\le \Pr\left[ \sum_{i = 1}^R r_i > \gamma Right] \ &\le \exp\left(- rac{(\gamma - \delta)R}{3}ight) \end{align*} by the multiplicative Chernoff bound. ootnote{The formulation we use here is as follows. Let $r_1, \dots, r_R$ be independent $\{0, 1\}$-valued random variables, $S = \sum_{i=1}^R r_i$, and $\mu = \mathbb{E}[S]$. Then for $\eta > 1$, we have $\Pr[S > (1+\eta) \mu] \le \exp(-\eta \mu / 3)$. In this application, we are taking $\mu \le \delta R$ and $\eta = \gamma R / \mu - 1 > 1$.} Thus, we have \[2 \sum_{x 
otin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \le \exp\left(- rac{(\gamma - \delta)R}{3}ight).\] Putting everything together, we see that Expression~\eqref{eqn:buttz} is at least $1 - \delta^R - \exp\left(-(\gamma - \delta) R / 3ight)$ as we wanted to show.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Split the correlation into the full AND-OR correlation minus off-domain mass; bound the first by one-sided error and the second by a Chernoff bound.

nodes.name: Split quantity
nodes.statement: We begin by observing that the quantity of interest can be written as \begin{align} &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - \nonumber \\ &\qquad\qquad \left( \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) + \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \right) \nonumber \\ \ge &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - 2 \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Split into AND-OR correlation and off-domain mass.

nodes.statement: &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - \nonumber \\ &\qquad\qquad \left( \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) + \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \right) \nonumber \\ \ge &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - 2 \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|.
nodes.name: Equation eqn:buttz
nodes.label: eqn:buttz

nodes.name: First term
nodes.statement: We estimate each term of Expression~\eqref{eqn:buttz} separately, beginning with the first term. Just as in the proofs of \Cref{prop:error-amp} and \Cref{prop:degree-amp}, we have \begin{align*} \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} (\Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot (\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N)(x) &= \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} \Phi(z) \cdot \mathbb{E}_y[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)] \end{align*} where $y \in \{-1,1\}^R$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes the value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. For $z = -\mathbf{1}$, we have by~\eqref{eqn:mybullshitequation} that $2 \sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 0$, so the contribution of the corresponding term to the sum is $1/2$. For $z = \mathbf{1}$, we use the fact that $2 \sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x)| \le \delta$ to compute \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathbb{E}_{y}[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i, \dots)] &= \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 2\Pr_y[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1 ] \right) \\ &\ge \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 2\delta^R\right). \end{align*} Hence, the first summand of~\eqref{eqn:buttz} is at least $1-\delta^R$.
nodes.statement_short: First term at least $1-\delta^R$ via one-sided error.

nodes.name: Second term rewrite
nodes.statement:
We now estimate the second summand, $2 \sum_{x 
otin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|$. As in the proofs of \Cref{prop:error-amp} and \Cref{prop:degree-amp}, we let $\lambda$ denote the distribution with probability mass function $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$. Then  egin{align*}\hspace{-2.2em} 2\sum_{x 
otin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| &= 2^{R+1} \mathbb{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes R}} [|\Phi(\dots, \operatorname{sgn} \psi(x_i), \dots)| \cdot \mathbb{I}(x 
otin G)] \ &= 2\sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} |\Phi(z)| \cdot \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z] \ &= \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{-1}] + \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{1}]. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite off-domain mass as conditional probabilities.

nodes.name: Sign vector -1
nodes.statement: We analyze each term of this sum separately. For the first term, observe that by one-sided error of $\psi$, it follows that if $x = (x_1, \dots, x_R)$ is any input $\operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = -1$ for all $i$ then $\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1$ for all $i$. Thus we are guaranteed that $x \in G$, so the contribution of the first summand is zero.
nodes.statement_short: For all-negative signs, $x\in G$.

nodes.name: Chernoff
nodes.statement: To analyze the second summand, let us denote by $r_i \in \{0, 1\}$ the indicator random variable for the event $\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1$ when $x_i$ is drawn from the conditional distribution $(\lambda | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = 1)$. Then \begin{align*} \Pr[r_i = 1] &= \Pr_{x_i \sim \lambda}[\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1 | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = 1] \\ &= 2\sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x_i)| \\ &\le \delta \end{align*} by~\eqref{eqn:mybullshitequation}. Hence, \begin{align*} \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x \notin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{1}] &\le \Pr\left[ \sum_{i = 1}^R r_i > \gamma R\right] \\ &\le \exp\left(-\frac{(\gamma - \delta)R}{3}\right) \end{align*} by the multiplicative Chernoff bound.\footnote{The formulation we use here is as follows. Let $r_1, \dots, r_R$ be independent $\{0, 1\}$-valued random variables, $S = \sum_{i=1}^R r_i$, and $\mu = \mathbb{E}[S]$. Then for $\eta > 1$, we have $\Pr[S > (1+\eta) \mu] \le \exp(-\eta \mu / 3)$. In this application, we are taking $\mu \le \delta R$ and $\eta = \gamma R / \mu - 1 > 1$.} Thus, we have \[2 \sum_{x \notin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \le \exp\left(-\frac{(\gamma - \delta)R}{3}\right).\]
nodes.statement_short: For all-positive signs, Chernoff bound.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Putting everything together, we see that Expression~\eqref{eqn:buttz} is at least $1 - \delta^R - \exp\left(-(\gamma - \delta) R / 3\right)$ as we wanted to show.
nodes.statement_short: Combine both estimates.

nodes.statement: It follows from a reduction in Ambainis et al. \cite[Section 6]{juntatesting} that for any $N=O(R)$ and sufficiently small constant $\gamma > 0$, a $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$ lower bound for the approximate degree or quantum query complexity of $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ implies an $\tilde{\Omega}(k^{1/2})$ approximate degree or quantum query lower bound for $k$-junta testing for proximity parameter $\varepsilon = 1/3$. Hence, \Cref{sethm} has the following corollary.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Ambainis et al.'s reduction from Image Size Testing to junta testing.

nodes.statement: Any quantum tester that distinguishes $k$-juntas from functions that are $(1/3)$-far from any $k$-junta with error probability at most $1/3$ makes $\tilde{\Omega}(k^{1/2})$ queries to the function.
nodes.name: Quantum lower bound for k-junta testing
assumptions: Any quantum tester that distinguishes $k$-juntas from functions that are $(1/3)$-far from any $k$-junta with error probability at most $1/3$
conclusions: makes $\tilde{\Omega}(k^{1/2})$ queries to the function

nodes.statement: Given an input $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]^N$, and $i \in [R]$, let $f_i = |\{j \colon s_j=i\}|$, and let $p$ be the probability distribution over $[R]$ such that $p_i=f_i/N$.
nodes.name: Distribution p of an input list

nodes.statement: Define $$\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{ if } \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^R |p_i - 1/R| \leq \gamma_1\\ 1 & \text{ if } \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^R |p_i - 1/R| \geq \gamma_2\\ \text{undefined} & \text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$ Above, $ \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^R |p_i - 1/R| $ is the statistical distance between $p$ and the uniform distribution.
nodes.name: Statistical distance from uniform function

nodes.statement: The $\mathsf{ SDU}$ problem reduces to $\mathsf{ IST}$ in the sense that any approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{ SDU}$ implies the existence of an approximation to $\mathsf{ IST}$ of the same degree. Hence, the approximate degree of $\mathsf{ SDU}$ is at least as large as that of $\mathsf{ IST}$. For intuition as to why this is true, let us relate $\mathsf{ IST}^{1/2}_{N, R}$ to $\mathsf{ SDU}^{1/2, 0}_{N, R}$ in the special case where $N = R$ and no dummy (i.e., 0) items appear in the input to $\mathsf{ IST}$. If $(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ is a true input to $\mathsf{ IST}^{1/2}_{N, R}$, i.e., $\mathsf{ IST}^{1/2}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$, then every index $i \in [R]$ must appear in the input list exactly once. Hence, the distribution represented by $(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ is exactly uniform, so $\mathsf{ SDU}^{1/2, 0}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$. On the other hand, if $\mathsf{ IST}^{1/2}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = 1$, then at most $R/2$ indices $i \in [R]$ appear in the input list, so the list represents a distribution with statistical distance at least $1/2$ from uniform. Thus, an approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{ SDU}^{1/2, 0}_{N, R}$ is also an approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{ IST}^{1/2}_{N, R}$.
nodes.name: SDU reduces to IST (intuition)
nodes.statement_short: An approximation for SDU yields one for IST of the same degree; illustrated for $N=R$ without dummy items.

nodes.statement: For some $N = O(R)$, and some constants $0 < \gamma_2 < \gamma_1 < 1$, $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}\left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right) \ge \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$. The same lower bound applies to the quantum query complexity of $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$.
nodes.name: Approximate degree lower bound for SDU
assumptions: For some $N = O(R)$, and some constants $0 < \gamma_2 < \gamma_1 < 1$
conclusions: $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}\left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right) \ge \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$
The same lower bound applies to the quantum query complexity of $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$
nodes.label: sduthm

nodes.statement: Fix $R >0$, let $c$ be the constant from \Cref{sethm}, $\gamma<(2/3c)^2$ be a sufficiently small constant, and $N= c \cdot \gamma^{-1/2} \cdot R$. As inputs in $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ are interpreted as elements of $[R]_0^N$, we can equivalently interpret them as elements of $[R+1]^N$, i.e., as inputs to $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$, for any desired $0 < \gamma_1 < \gamma_2 < 1$. Set $\gamma_1 = 1-3\gamma/2$ and $\gamma_2=1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$. Observe that since $\gamma < (2/3c)^2$, $\gamma_1$ is strictly greater than $\gamma_2$. We claim that \begin{align*} &\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1) \subseteq \left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right)^{-1}(-1), \text{ and} \\ &\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(+1) \subseteq \left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right)^{-1}(+1). \end{align*} Indeed, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$, with all probabilities being integer multiples of $1/N=\gamma^{1/2}/(cR)$, the statistical distance between any such distribution and the uniform distribution is at most $1-R/N = 1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$. This follows from the following calculation. Amongst probability distributions $(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$ and all probabilities $p_i$ being integer multiples of $1/N$, it is not hard to see that one maximizes the statistical distance from the uniform distribution over $[R+1]$ by setting $p_1=1-\frac{R-1}{N}$, $p_2=p_3 = \dots = p_{R}=1/N$, and $p_{R+1}=0$. The statistical distance from uniform is: \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \left( \left(1-\frac{R-1}{N}-\frac{1}{R+1}\right) + \left(R-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R+1} - \frac1N\right) + \frac{1}{R+1} \right)\\ = 1-\frac{R}{N} + \frac1N - \frac{1}{R+1} \leq 1-\frac{R}{N}, \end{align*} where we have assumed that $N \geq R+1$, which is true for sufficiently small choice of $\gamma$. Similarly, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at most $\gamma \cdot R +1$, the statistical distance between any such distribution and the uniform distribution is at least $1-3\gamma/2$. To see this, let $p=(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ be any distribution of support size at most $\gamma \cdot R$, and let $S = \{i \colon p_i=0\}$ and $\bar{S}$ be the complement of $S$. Then the statistical distance of $p$ from uniform is at least \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \left(\sum_{i \in S} \left(p_i - \frac{1}{R+1} \right) \right) + \frac{1}{2} \left(\sum_{i \in \bar{S}} \left( p_i - \frac{1}{R+1} \right) \right) = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{|S|}{R+1} + \left(\sum_{i \in \bar{S}} p_i\right) - \frac{|\bar{S}|}{R+1}\right)\\ = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{|S|}{R+1} + 1 - \frac{|\bar{S}|}{R+1}\right) \geq \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{(1-\gamma) R}{R+1} + 1 - \frac{\gamma R + 1}{R+1}\right) = \frac{1}{2} \left(1 + \frac{R-2\gamma R - 1}{R+1}\right)\\ = 1 - \frac{\gamma R + 1}{R+1} = 1 - \gamma - \frac{\gamma + 1}{R+1} \geq 1-3\gamma/2. \end{align*} It is an easy consequence of the above that any $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial of degree $d$ for $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ implies an approximation to $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ of the same degree (i.e., that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}) \leq d$). \Cref{sduthm} then follows from \Cref{sethm}.
nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement_short: Reduction: interpret IST inputs as distributions; full image implies distance at most $1-R/N$ and small image implies distance at least $1-3\gamma/2$.

nodes.name: Parameters
nodes.statement: Fix $R >0$, let $c$ be the constant from \Cref{sethm}, $\gamma<(2/3c)^2$ be a sufficiently small constant, and $N= c \cdot \gamma^{-1/2} \cdot R$. nodes.name: Inclusion of preimages
nodes.statement: We claim that \begin{align*} &\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1) \subseteq \left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right)^{-1}(-1), \text{ and} \\ &\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(+1) \subseteq \left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right)^{-1}(+1). \end{align*} Indeed, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$, with all probabilities being integer multiples of $1/N=\gamma^{1/2}/(cR)$, the statistical distance between any such distribution and the uniform distribution is at most $1-R/N = 1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$. This follows from the following calculation. Amongst probability distributions $(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$ and all probabilities $p_i$ being integer multiples of $1/N$, it is not hard to see that one maximizes the statistical distance from the uniform distribution over $[R+1]$ by setting $p_1=1-\frac{R-1}{N}$, $p_2=p_3 = \dots = p_{R}=1/N$, and $p_{R+1}=0$. The statistical distance from uniform is: \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \left( \left(1-\frac{R-1}{N}-\frac{1}{R+1}\right) + \left(R-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R+1} - \frac1N\right) + \frac{1}{R+1} \right)\\ = 1-\frac{R}{N} + \frac1N - \frac{1}{R+1} \leq 1-\frac{R}{N}, \end{align*} where we have assumed that $N \geq R+1$, which is true for sufficiently small choice of $\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: IST preimages are contained in SDU preimages.

nodes.name: Full image is close
nodes.statement: Indeed, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$, with all probabilities being integer multiples of $1/N=\gamma^{1/2}/(cR)$, the statistical distance between any such distribution and the uniform distribution is at most $1-R/N = 1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$.
nodes.statement_short: Full support means distance at most $1-R/N$.

nodes.name: Extremal distribution
nodes.statement: This follows from the following calculation. Amongst probability distributions $(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$ and all probabilities $p_i$ being integer multiples of $1/N$, it is not hard to see that one maximizes the statistical distance from the uniform distribution over $[R+1]$ by setting $p_1=1-\frac{R-1}{N}$, $p_2=p_3 = \dots = p_{R}=1/N$, and $p_{R+1}=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the extremal distribution.

nodes.name: Compute distance
nodes.statement: The statistical distance from uniform is: \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \left( \left(1-\frac{R-1}{N}-\frac{1}{R+1}\right) + \left(R-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R+1} - \frac1N\right) + \frac{1}{R+1} \right)\\ = 1-\frac{R}{N} + \frac1N - \frac{1}{R+1} \leq 1-\frac{R}{N}, \end{align*} where we have assumed that $N \geq R+1$, which is true for sufficiently small choice of $\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute its distance.

nodes.name: Small image is far
nodes.statement: Similarly, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at most $\gamma \cdot R +1$, the statistical distance between any such distribution and the uniform distribution is at least $1-3\gamma/2$. To see this, let $p=(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ be any distribution of support size at most $\gamma \cdot R$, and let $S = \{i \colon p_i=0\}$ and $\bar{S}$ be the complement of $S$. Then the statistical distance of $p$ from uniform is at least \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \left(\sum_{i \in S} \left(p_i - \frac{1}{R+1} \right) \right) + \frac{1}{2} \left(\sum_{i \in \bar{S}} \left( p_i - \frac{1}{R+1} \right) \right) = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{|S|}{R+1} + \left(\sum_{i \in \bar{S}} p_i\right) - \frac{|\bar{S}|}{R+1}\right)\\ = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{|S|}{R+1} + 1 - \frac{|\bar{S}|}{R+1}\right) \geq \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{(1-\gamma) R}{R+1} + 1 - \frac{\gamma R + 1}{R+1}\right) = \frac{1}{2} \left(1 + \frac{R-2\gamma R - 1}{R+1}\right)\\ = 1 - \frac{\gamma R + 1}{R+1} = 1 - \gamma - \frac{\gamma + 1}{R+1} \geq 1-3\gamma/2. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Small support means distance at least $1-3\gamma/2$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: It is an easy consequence of the above that any $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial of degree $d$ for $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ implies an approximation to $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ of the same degree (i.e., that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}) \leq d$). \Cref{sduthm} then follows from \Cref{sethm}.
nodes.statement_short: Approximations for SDU give ones for IST; apply the IST bound.

nodes.statement: Given a distribution $p$ over $[R]$, the Shannon entropy of $p$, denoted $H(p)$, is defined to be $H(p):=\sum_{i \in [R]} p_i \log_2(1/p_i)$.
nodes.name: Shannon entropy
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation

nodes.statement: Following Goldreich and Vadhan \cite{goldreichvadhansurvey}, we define a partial function $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}_{N, R}^{\alpha, \beta}$ capturing the problem of comparing the entropies of two distributions. The function $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}_{N, R}^{\alpha, \beta}$ takes as input two vectors in $[R]^N$ and interprets each vector $i \in \{1, 2\}$ as a probability distribution $p_i$ over $[R]$, with $p_i(j)=f_{i,j}/N$ where $f_{i,j}$ is the frequency of $j$ in the $i$th vector. The function $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}_{N, R}^{\alpha, \beta}$ evaluates to $$\begin{cases} -1 & \text{ if } H(p_1)-H(p_2) \leq \beta\\ 1 & \text{ if } H(p_1)-H(p_2) \geq \alpha \\ \text{undefined} & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$
nodes.name: Entropy comparison function GapCmprEnt
nodes.statement_short: Partial function on two input lists: $-1$ if the entropy difference is at most $\beta$, $+1$ if at least $\alpha$.
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation

nodes.statement: There exist constants $0 < \beta < \alpha < 1$ such that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{N, R}) = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2}).$ The same lower bound applies to the quantum query complexity of $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{N, R}$.
nodes.name: Approximate degree lower bound for entropy comparison
conclusions: $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{N, R}) = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2}).$
The same lower bound applies to the quantum query complexity of $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{N, R}$

nodes.label: entropysucks

nodes.statement: Vadhan \cite[Claim 4.4.2 and Remark 4.4.3]{vadhan} showed that as long as $H( (1+\gamma_1)/2) < 1-\gamma_2 - \lambda$, then $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ is reducible to $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$ for some constants $\alpha, \beta$ such that $\alpha-\beta=\lambda$. This reduction (described next for completeness) implies that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}) \leq \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R})$. For completeness, we sketch this transformation, closely following the presentation of Goldreich and Vadhan \cite{goldreichvadhansurvey}. At a high level, the reduction transforms an input in $[R]^N$ to $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ (interpreted as a distribution $p$ over $[R]$) into two distributions $p_1, p_2$ over $[R] \times \{0, 1\}$ as follows. Both $p_1$ and $p_2$ start by sampling an $s \in \{0, 1\}$ at random. If $s=0$, then a random sample $r$ is chosen from $p$, and if $s=1$, then $r$ is set to a uniform random sample from $[R]$. Distribution $p_2$ outputs $(r, s)$, while $p_1$ outputs $(r, b)$ for a random $b \in \{0, 1\}$. The entropy of $p_1$ is always $v + 1$, where $v=\frac{1}{2} H(p) + \frac{1}{2} \log_2(R)$. As for the entropy of $p_2$, if $p$ is far from the uniform distribution, then the selection bit $s$ will be essentially determined by the sample $r$. Hence, the entropy of $p_2$ will be approximately $v$, which is noticeably smaller than the entropy of $p_1$. On the other hand, if the two input distributions are close then (even conditioned on the sample selected) the selection bit $s$ will be almost random and so $H(p_2) \approx v+1$, which is approximately the same as $H(p_1)$. Quantitatively, Vadhan \cite{vadhan} shows that if the statistical distance between $p$ and the uniform distribution is $\delta$, then $1-\delta \leq H(p_1) - H(p_2) \leq H( (1+\delta)/2)$. Since we are considering distributions specified as vectors in $[R]^N$, this transformation can be equivalently described as follows. Assume for simplicity that $R$ divides $N$. If $p$ is specified by a vector $u$ in $[R]^N$, then $p_2$ is specified by a vector $w$ in $([R]\times\{0,1\})^{4N}$ defined as follows. For all $i \in [N]$ and $j \in \{0, 1\}$, $w_{i, j}=(u_i, 0)$, and for $j \in \{2, 3\}$, $w_{i, j}=(\lceil Ri/N\rceil, 1)$. Similarly, $p_1$ is specified by a vector $v$ in $([R]\times\{0,1\})^{4N}$. For $i \in [R]$ and $j \in \{0, 1\}$, $v_{i, j}=(u_i, j)$, and for $j \in \{2, 3\}$, $v_{i, j} = (\lceil Ri/N\rceil, j-2)$. Observe that when representing $u$, $v$, and $w$ as vectors in $\{-1,1\}^{N \log_2(R)}$ or $\{-1,1\}^{4N \cdot \log_2(R)}$, each bit of $v$ and $w$ depends on at most one bit of $u$. Recall that in the statement of \Cref{sduthm}, $\gamma_1 = 1-3\gamma/2$ and $\gamma_2=1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$, where $\gamma$ is an arbitrary constant less than $(2/3c)^2$, where $c>1$ is the constant from \Cref{sethm}. Clearly, $H( (1+\gamma_1)/2)) = H(1-3 \gamma/4) = H(3 \gamma/4)$. Using the fact that for any $p \in [0, 1/2]$, \begin{align*} H(p) &= -p \log_2(p) - (1-p) \log_2(1-p) \\ &\le -2p\log_2(p) \\ &\le 6p^{3/4}, \end{align*} it follows that for some constant $\gamma \le 1/648c^4$, we have $H(3 \gamma/4) < \gamma^{1/2}/c$. Hence, Vadhan's reduction from $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ to $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$ applies to this setting of $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$, and this shows that any degree $d$ $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$ implies a degree $d$ polynomial $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$. Combined with \Cref{sduthm}, this implies that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}) = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2}).$

nodes.statement_short: Vadhan's reduction from SDU to entropy comparison, implemented by a transformation where each output bit depends on one input bit.

nodes.statement: Clearly, a quantum query algorithm that approximates entropy up to additive error $(\alpha-\beta)/4$ can be used to solve $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$, by (approximately) computing the entropies of each of the two input distributions, and determining whether the difference is at most $(\beta + \alpha)/2$. Hence, \Cref{entropysucks} implies the following lower bound for approximating entropy to additive error $\alpha-\beta$.

nodes.statement: Let $N=c \cdot R$ for a sufficiently large constant $c$. Interpret an input in $[R]^N$ as a distribution $p$ in the natural way (i.e., for each $j \in [R]$, $p_j=f_j/N$, where $f_j$ is the number of times $j$ appears in the input). There is a constant $\varepsilon > 0$ such that any quantum algorithm that approximates the entropy of $p$ up to additive error $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $2/3$ requires $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$ queries.
